The Fourth Intermediate General Assembly of the Institute, held in Bethlehem (from 21 November 1993 to 16 January 1994), set itself, among other working objectives, that of “offering a renewed formulation of the outline of the Treatise of Spiritual Doctrine1 starting from the aspects of the mystery of the poor Christ” brought out:

  • in the book “God's Gift to Rosa Gattorno”, drawn up on the basis of the spiritual Memoirs written by Mother Rosa;

  • in the Rule of 1869, written by Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore;

  • and in our present Constitutions.

When the work was finished, the Assembly expressed its gratitude to the Lord and its deep desire that the Treatise of Spiritual Doctrine be produced soon, in order to unify the formation journey of the whole charismatic Family, raised up by the Holy Spirit in the Church through Rosa Gattorno and carried on in time by all who follow her.

⟦p. 8⟧

In response to this desire, it was my firm resolve to spare no effort to fulfil the Assembly's request in due time.

1 Cf. FIGLIE DI S. ANNA, Il Dono di Dio a Rosa Gattorno, Rome 1994, p. 12; Acts of the Fourth Intermediate General Assembly 1994, pp. 30-31.

Therefore, after consulting Fr. Anselmo Dalbesio OFM Cap., an expert in Sacred Scripture, and having verified that the outline of the Treatise was soundly set in a biblical perspective, we entrusted its writing to the Very Rev. Don Luigi Bogliolo, S.D.B., an expert in philosophy and spiritual theology.

Our gratitude goes to him for faithfully developing the themes proposed to him and for welcoming our collaboration, so that the distinctive character of the charism the Lord has given to every son and daughter of Saint Anne and to the members of the Movement of Hope might shine clearly through the contents.

Thanks to his readiness, I am now able, together with my dearest Assistants, to fulfil the promise already made during the Eighteenth General Chapter and repeated at the Fourth Intermediate General Assembly, by handing the present text to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne and to all the Aggregations and Associations.

The Treatise on Spirituality is in fact addressed to all the members of the Family of Saint Anne, mother of Mary Immaculate.2

⟦p. 9⟧

The text gathers a synthesis of the values we are called to contemplate and live. We cannot authentically live the charism the Father has given to each of us unless we know the story of God with the foundress.

Her experience of God, left as a legacy in many writings and in the witness of her life, is the most luminous interpretation of the charism for her disciples.

2 Cf. Il Dono di Dio a Rosa Gattorno, op. cit., p. 14.

The Treatise in fact presents all the charismatic dimensions that reflect the divine and spiritual realities she contemplated and experienced as transforming presences: the Mystery of the poor Christ and of the Most Holy Trinity, the presence of Mary, their perfect image, and that of Saint Anne, intimately associated with her Immaculate Daughter.

The aim of the Treatise, therefore, is to help us live intensely and faithfully the “Gift” the Father has given us in Christ, a gift that finds the light it needs in the charism of Rosa Gattorno.3

The new text therefore spurs us further to improve the quality of our spiritual life at the personal, community and family level. May Christ Jesus, in the mystery of his poverty, shine in the face and the works of every son and daughter of Saint Anne and of every member of the Movement of Hope.

May people recognise through our witness the fatherhood of God, who floods us with mercy in Christ Jesus and in the Spirit, and who gives us in Mary, daughter of Saint Anne, the fullness of the old Covenant-Hope and the luminous dawn of the new, the perfect model of total sharing in his saving plan fulfilled in the Son: Priest, Victim and first fruits of those risen from the dead.

Sr. A. Virginia Sinagra, Superior General

3 Ibidem, pp. 18-24.

A treatise, or perhaps better a handbook of spiritual life and doctrine for the Daughters of Saint Anne and for the great Family that recognises itself in the spirit and charism of the foundress Mother Rosa Gattorno, cannot be reduced to a dry treatise of theology. A text of this kind must contain concrete norms of spiritual life, able to guide souls day after day towards perfection in the sense understood and taught by Mother Rosa Gattorno.

It is therefore essentially a matter of following a precise method to set out a particular charism, one with its own features that distinguish it from, and at the same time unite it with, the other great Families devoted to holiness and the apostolate.

Mother Rosa's charism has been officially approved by the Church. This gives assurance to all who embrace it, drawn by God.

The task of this treatise is therefore to outline, as faithfully as possible, the spiritual inheritance left by the foundress in her writings, her example and her apostolate…, a spiritual inheritance of singular, God-inspired originality.

Every form of Christian spirituality, however, falls within the classic and complex framework of the truths revealed by God and is lived against the background of the common doctrine of the Catholic Church.

⟦p. 12⟧

In the schools of Catholic Theology there is a body of theoretical and practical treatises founded on the Revelation God made to Abraham, to the Patriarchs, to the Prophets of the Old Testament and, definitively and completely, to us through Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word, the Son of God.

⟦p. 13⟧

Theology comprises a body of treatises that study the distinct revealed truths. First of all there is a central treatise devoted to the revealed truths themselves, apart from their practical application. This treatise is normally called “dogmatic theology”. The word “dogma” means “teaching”, and dogmas are the truths taught by God and professed by us in the Creed. The name “dogmatic” theology does not, however, mean truth imposed, but truths offered to us kindly by the condescending goodness of God. We accept these truths by faith, relying on the authority of God. Reason on its own, with its own feeble strength, could never come to know them. Spiritual theology is therefore entirely founded on revealed truths. “Fundamental theology”, on the other hand, studies the motives of credibility, the arguments that make the truths professed in the Creed historically verifiable and acceptable, since our assent to the faith must also be rational. It is therefore a rather introductory study, which opens the way to theology proper. First, in fact, one must become aware of the duty to believe: “I would not believe if I did not see that I must believe”. Faith has such historical foundations that it must be accepted as an indisputable historical event, at the centre of which stand the birth, life, passion, death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

Since God created man free, and therefore master and cause of his own acts, we need to know clearly what is good for the growth and development of the person, what keeps the person at the height of his dignity, and what instead degrades him.

Man needs sure and clear norms and rules for his conduct.

From creation God inscribed in the human heart the laws of moral activity, but man's intellect and will are often ensnared by the devil.

A more explicit legislation was therefore needed, especially after the original fall. This is what God did in revealing the ten commandments to Moses, a sure guide for practical human activity.

Man does not grow only physically like the lower animals; he can and must grow morally throughout his life and strengthen himself in right conduct. Moral growth therefore has no limits.

The part of theology that studies precisely the laws of right conduct and of the development of the human and Christian personality is called “moral theology”.

While revealed truths come to the help of the intellect, the commandments come to meet the will.

If “dogmatic” theology is essentially theoretical, “moral” theology is practical.

⟦p. 14⟧

Human freedom, which God respects supremely, because freedom alone makes it possible to choose and to distinguish what is good from what is not, what helps the development of the personality from what harms and degrades it, is the object of “moral” theology.

How is “moral theology” connected with “spiritual theology”, and how does it differ from it, and vice versa?

“Spiritual” theology presupposes “moral” theology and is connected with it as the seed is with the flower and the ripe fruit.

Spiritual theology too is the study of personal relations with God, but carried to the fullness of perfection. Jesus Christ himself, answering and guiding the young man who questioned him, defined, as it were, in a wonderful way the connection and the distinction between moral and spiritual theology.

“Someone came up to him and said, ‘Good Teacher, what good must I do to obtain eternal life?’ He answered, ‘Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you wish to enter into eternal life, keep the commandments.’ He asked, ‘Which ones?’ Jesus answered, ‘You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, honour your father and your mother, love your neighbour as yourself.’ The young man said to him, ‘I have always kept all these; what do I still lack?’ Jesus said to him, ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.’ When he heard this, the young man went away sad, for he had great possessions” (Matt 19:16-22).

⟦p. 15⟧

In this short episode we find clearly outlined the essential tasks of the Christian moral life (which the young man says he has always practised) and those of the spiritual life, whose fundamental principles Jesus himself sets out.

The episode, dense with meaning as Jesus' words always are, states clearly what the essence of the life of perfection consists in, embraced both by those who give themselves wholly to the Lord through the profession of the evangelical counsels and by all who follow its spirit according to their own state of life.

Spiritual theology further comprises two distinct phases: the “ascetical” and the “mystical”.

Detachment from the world and its goods is called asceticism or ascetical theology, and it is the part that teaches the various aspects and degrees of detachment.

Mystical theology, on the other hand, teaches us to follow Jesus, that is, to be united and identified ever more with him. This part of spiritual theology is called “mystical” also because it lives and studies the mysterious (mystical) union with God.

“Ascetics” by its nature tends to remove the obstacles that prevent or delay union with God. This, in fact, is precisely the crucial point of the spiritual life.

⟦p. 16⟧

In the first phase the good will of the creature is decisive, the will that was lacking in the case of the rich young man. In the second, “mystical” phase, good will, once the soul has gained total victory over its faults, at times remains passive, waiting for the movement of the Holy Spirit. This is the degree the mystics call the prayer “of quiet” or “passive” prayer.

The more faithful, generous and constant a soul is in loving God, the more the Holy Spirit acts, enlightening it and, in great mystics such as Mother Rosa, guiding it in an extraordinary way. Union with God can reach such a point that Jesus' words no longer cause wonder: “be perfect as your Father in heaven is perfect” (Matt 5:48).

The soul guided by the Holy Spirit can rise to dizzying heights, as Mother Rosa clearly did, as Saint Catherine of Siena, Saint Teresa of Avila, Saint John of the Cross and so many other saints in the Church were able to do. Here appear the depth and beauty of spiritual life and doctrine, which include the various degrees of union and prayer described by the mystical masters and doctors, among whom Saint Catherine of Siena and Saint Teresa of Avila stand out, declared “doctors” of the Church.

Following these paths, we look to such masters and mistresses without ever aspiring to extraordinary things, because everything that has been said and can be said about the spiritual life can happen in an entirely normal way, union with God being a wholly interior experience. What matters, however, is faithfulness in using the means of sanctification: the sacraments and prayer.

⟦p. 17⟧

As for Mother Rosa, Fr. Lázaro Iriarte, OFM Cap., in the volume “The Spiritual Profile of Rosa Gattorno”, has well described and commented on the mystical prayer and the various, certainly not ordinary, phenomena of the foundress. In this sense Mother Rosa too is an excellent teacher of modern spiritual life, and if she could speak to us today she would certainly say: learn to unite the apostolate well with contemplation. That is enough. For whoever tends resolutely towards holiness, Jesus Christ is everything. Whoever truly follows him tends, in prayer and in the apostolate, to reach the final goal of the Christian spiritual life: that Jesus may truly be “all in all” (Col 3:11).

Jesus lived detachment from the world and from himself in absolute fullness, even to death on a cross, in total and joyful adherence to the Father's will.

Christian spirituality then consists precisely in this full conformity with God's will, setting no limit to him. And when Jesus Christ becomes everything for a person, and the person becomes one with Jesus Christ, that person thereby becomes one with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

“Be perfect as your Father in heaven is perfect”: what depth, yet what simplicity in these words! Whoever truly loves Jesus Christ no longer finds anything burdensome in life.

Spiritual theology therefore teaches us to love Jesus Christ to the point of being ready even for martyrdom (death on a cross), making him not only our truth and our life (as he has always been for all humanity), but also our way, our supreme model.

⟦p. 18⟧

In this no one followed him more closely, and no one walked the way of the cross so sublimely and so generously, as Mary Most Holy, whom Mother Rosa contemplated as associated with the mystery of Christ the Redeemer.

Every charism is a gift, a particular sharing in the life, passion and death of Jesus. He is the source, the most perfect and unattainable model of Christian spiritual life and doctrine. Through him and in him the whole spiritual life unfolds within the three divine Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Jesus Christ is the infinite abyss of all virtues and all perfections. In him are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3). Jesus Christ must become “all in all” (Col 3:11); he is the beginning, the end, the substance, the synthesis of the spiritual life.

Knowing how Mother Rosa was able to imitate and love Jesus Christ is the substance of a treatise on spiritual life for the Family she founded.

And just as Jesus openly declares, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfil” (Matt 5:17), so every renewal is authentic to the extent that the Family returns to its first source, that is, to the spirit, to the oral and written teachings and, even more, to the example of the life lived by the Foundress in the charismatic genuineness willed by the Lord. Every charism has an unrepeatable singularity, because God never repeats himself in his works, and there is no person without a unique originality. This holds all the more for charisms, whether personal or at the foundational and community level, as Mother Rosa's charism was and is.

⟦p. 19⟧

This charism of hers and of her Family, born of the Holy Spirit, has an unrepeatable originality.

The teachings and examples of evangelical radicalism lived by Mother Rosa are its only and best commentary. Therefore, the more deeply the concrete facts of her interior life and of the way she loved Jesus Christ are explored, the more authentic her following will be, and the more it will renew communities and individuals.

We know, moreover, that the synthesis of the Christian spiritual life, as it emerges from the Gospels, is charity; indeed, that Jesus is charity itself made flesh.

The works founded by Mother Rosa are a clear application of Jesus' words and parables on charity. Thanks to the spread of the Institute throughout the world, this charity continues to work through Mother Rosa's spiritual Daughters and through those who follow her apostolic zeal. The exercise of supernatural and theological charity makes life not an ecstasy that carries one out of the senses, but an ecstasy that commits daily life to the service of God and neighbour.

⟦p. 20⟧

The ecstasy of sacrifice then becomes not an extraordinary phenomenon but an ordinary fact of daily life. It makes a person generously ready for sacrifice, for that kind of heroism which coincides with holiness. What matters, however, is not the extraordinary, granted to souls called to an extraordinary vocation such as Mother Rosa's. For her Daughters, and for all who follow her in the various states of life, the ordinary ecstasy of generous self-giving, always ready for sacrifice, is enough.

At this point the question of the difference between Christian spirituality and other, non-Christian forms of spirituality, such as Buddhist or Muslim spirituality, is easily resolved: in non-Christian spiritualities Jesus Christ is missing, and so theological and supernatural charity is missing. There may also be good elements, deriving from the natural law inscribed in the human heart in the very act of creation, but the most important presence is lacking: Jesus Christ, true God and true Man. That is why the divine Redeemer commands his Apostles: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt 28:19).

And since the essence of Christian spirituality consists in the most intimate possible union with Jesus Christ, Doctors and Fathers of the Church place Christian perfection in the very perfection of charity. That is why Saint Paul does not hesitate to say that charity is the most perfect of all charisms, because it puts us in direct contact with God himself, even though it is true that faith and hope open the door and point the way.

Whoever loves God already begins on earth the life of heaven. The only difference lies in the imperfection of seeing by faith, for in heaven we shall see him unveiled, “face to face”. In the beatific vision, therefore, faith and hope will cease, because there will be the immediate and full possession of God himself, in sight and in union.

⟦p. 21⟧

The other virtues will therefore come to an end; charity will continue, magnified and made a beatifying light, for ever.

While we are on earth we can therefore progress in the love of God day after day, without limit. Charity makes God truly reign in the heart and moves a person to give himself generously for the salvation of others.

Charity is therefore the universal vocation of all Christians, a vocation that will find its ineffable fulfilment in heaven.

Clearly a whole treatise on the spiritual life could be written by commenting on the nature and effects of charity. The same can be said of prayer, which after the sacraments is the great and sure means of leading the soul to the summit of the perfection of charity, especially when prayer becomes habitual, a living sense of the presence of God.

Loving contact with God, though still veiled, gives the soul a beginning, still partial and enigmatic, of that wholly unveiled and intoxicating vision which is eternal life in God.

Total dedication to the love of God and neighbour transforms Christian life into an uninterrupted ecstasy of love, it is worth repeating, and makes a person ready for any sacrifice, even to give one's life, especially when it is a matter of working for the spiritual good of souls. Countless holy men and women who enrich the history of the Church bear witness to this, together with Mother Rosa.

⟦p. 22⟧

Two expressions Mother Rosa habitually used clearly reveal the heights of her mystical union with God: the Crucifix is “my only good”, so Jesus crucified was everything in her life; and the other: “prayer is my only treasure”.

The asceticism of detachment, worked by poverty, humility and dedication to the service of God and neighbour, had therefore brought her ascetical and mystical spiritual life to wonderfully high levels.

We cannot deny it: we are living through a season of crisis of faith that affects Christendom.

Yet amid so many indifferent and superficial people there are in the world people thirsting for interiority. It is a thirst rooted in human nature itself, driven from within to seek God. At the root of all human aspirations lies the natural desire for God, the source, end and supreme truth for the human intellect and the highest good of the will. One glance within the Catholic Church is enough to see what is happening, especially since the Second Vatican Council. Many movements have arisen that seek a less superficial Christian life, aimed at living the Gospel in its fullness. These are deep ferments and vast “spiritual” movements that want to live Christianity, or rather the Gospel, seriously, so much so that they closely recall the fervour of the Church's first days.

A serious search for spirituality is evident in those who join the various “secular institutes” that have recently arisen in the Church. Even some people consecrated to God in the active life, through various forms of apostolate, not infrequently express the desire for a deeper interiority, more given to prayer and contemplation.

⟦p. 24⟧

Saint Thomas, the great doctor of the Church, asking whether the contemplative life or the active life of the apostolate is more perfect, replied: the most perfect religious life is the mixed life, that is, the contemplative life that radiates in apostolic action.

The irrepressible fullness of the interior life overflows like a river in flood into the outward life of the apostolate for the salvation of souls, without losing anything of its inner richness.

Authentic spirituality always reveals a great love for God that necessarily involves love of neighbour. Mother Rosa Gattorno, by her life, works, teachings and writings, is an unsurpassed model of this spirituality. Her writings and teachings reveal in her a true teacher of spiritual doctrine, one that finds its beginning, development and conclusion in the love of God and neighbour.

An active life of apostolate uprooted from a strong interior life does not exist and is not possible. The fact that Mother Rosa was endowed with an uncommon richness of mystical life is the most eloquent proof of her spirit made active in the tireless work of her foundations and initiatives, which have left in the Church and in the world a very deep mark, rich in holiness and in apostolic labour for the human and spiritual good of countless souls. This is also the deep reason for the remarkable growth of her Institute in the world and its unstoppable development.

⟦p. 25⟧

If there is a historical model of Christian spirituality that stands out among others, it is Mother Rosa's charism. The flourishing vitality of her spiritual Family is concrete proof of this.

The wonderful union of life, prayer and contemplation, of spontaneous readiness to embrace and live with courage, and even with enthusiasm, sufferings, crosses and contradictions, is a strong reminder to all Christians of the solemn principle stated by Jesus: “without me you can do nothing”; with me you can work miracles, you can move mountains, you can enlighten and warm the world with the love of God and neighbour and transform it. In this light Mother Rosa's charism shines radiantly, and it is no wonder that it has been understood, has fascinated and continues to attract people well disposed to welcome the light of her ideal, so faithful to the life and teaching of Jesus that they live it and teach others to live it in female and male religious life, in the contemplative life, in the secular institute and in the “Movement of Hope”.

In this perspective the Foundress's charism takes on meaning in all its details.

Her charism is “Christ in the mystery of his poverty” and of his passion, contemplated in Mary, his perfect image, and in Saint Anne, mother of Mary, the link between the old and the new Covenant and Hope.

This charism, single yet rich, has many aspects and manifold expressions, as its history shows and as we shall see in the following pages.

⟦p. 26⟧

Strictly biblical and evangelical in character, it is marked by unmistakable particular features that identify it and clearly distinguish it from other charisms that arose before, during or after the earthly life of Mother Rosa Gattorno. It is no wonder, therefore, that a charism so firmly anchored in these principles can truly project itself into the future with the very vitality of the Gospel; it will surely remain a shining beacon in the history of the Church and of religious life, lit by the inexhaustible source of the Gospel light.

For the charismatic Family inspired by her, the presence of Saint Anne is a clear reminder of her spirituality as mother of the Immaculate, a spirituality in which the spirituality of the OT itself reaches its conclusion and full realisation.

In Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate, the two distinct but inseparable spiritualities meet: that of the old and that of the new Covenant. The old Covenant, personified in its fullness by Saint Anne; the new Covenant, personified sublimely by her whom the Angel will greet: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you”, as he never has been and never will be with any other creature, human or angelic. “The Lord is with you” to the point that the eternal Word, becoming flesh, raises her to be Mother of a Son who will be at the same time, from eternity, from always, truly Son of the Eternal Father and, in time, truly Son of Mary.

⟦p. 30⟧

Into this great mystery of Mary's divine motherhood fits the exceptional figure of Saint Anne, from whom springs, with the Immaculate her Daughter, the splendid dawn that announces joy to the whole world, to the whole history of humanity.

1.1. God reveals himself in history

The charismatic grace of Saint Anne sums up the spirituality of the old Covenant, marked by Hope in the promised Redeemer, a promise guaranteed by the pact of Covenant repeatedly made by God with Abraham, the Patriarchs and the Prophets, and sealed by resounding wonders through which he wished to assure his divine assistance and guarantee the fulfilment of his promises. God creates man in grace and therefore in hope, on two levels: that of creation and that of elevation to the dignity of a son.

Saint Thomas Aquinas explains that, having been created with an intellectual (and therefore spiritual) nature, on this ground alone man deserves, among all the creatures of this sensible world, the name of son of God, thanks to his spiritual soul, though still on the level of creation. The human intellect by nature thirsts for truth, and the will for good; not, however, for a limited truth or good, because intellect and will know no limits in their striving towards the true and the good.

⟦p. 31⟧

Intellect and will ultimately tend towards absolute Truth and Goodness. In this thirst, inborn in man's spiritual nature, lies what theologians call the “natural desire for God”.

The human person, then, because endowed with intellect and will, is made by virtue of creation to know and love God. Yet with created powers alone no creature could ever reach him.

Left on the level of mere created nature, human life would have been like the suffering of an exile sick with homesickness, never soothed by a return home. That is why God never left man in the state of pure nature. He came at once to meet him, making him a sharer in his own divine nature. So he did with Adam, raised at once to the supernatural order, that is, to a life immensely higher than that of creation: to the state of grace. This state, however, did not deprive Adam of freedom of choice, as indeed God had done with the angels.

Adam, however, used his own will against the will of God, disobeying the Creator, and since he was the head of humanity, all men were virtually present in this first root of human nature. All men descended from the stock of Adam and Eve were stained by that original fault and would never have returned to the state of grace without the work of the Redeemer. God came to meet fallen man with divine magnificence, promising the Messiah (Gen 3:15) and sending his own Son to take upon himself that human nature in which all men were virtually and eminently included and brought back to a state of grace higher than the former one.

⟦p. 32⟧

All men were raised again to a dignity incomparably higher than before, with respect for the will of each. Before God there is no anonymity of a mass of individuals making up a family, a class or a people. The mass, the whole, the totality is something abstract, non-existent, even though there is a spiritual and moral bond that makes of it one family: the human family. Before God, therefore, there stands first of all the individual, the person in his unrepeatable singularity.

And since people influence one another in good and in evil, there is also the malign action of the first tempter, the devil, who with serpentine cunning tempts man to evil and works with fierce persistence and tireless malice to win crowds and nations over to evil.

Hence God's choice of a people that would remain faithful to him, acting according to his will in view of the Redeemer's coming. For this purpose he chose Abraham and asked of him an exceptional proof of obedience, ordering him to sacrifice to him his only son, Isaac. It was truly a supreme human proof of “faithfulness” to God, almost a prelude to the supreme proof of obedience of the future Redeemer (Gen 22:1-18). Abraham obeys and God at once rewards him twice over: sparing his only son and making him father of a people as numerous as the stars of the sky and the sand of the sea.

⟦p. 33⟧

The chosen people will be Israel, one immense family from which the future Redeemer will be born. A people closely united by a promise: the promise of a victory in which the head of the serpent will be crushed, the serpent that hurled man into the abyss of sin, turning the earthly paradise into a valley of tears.

The history of the chosen people thus unfolds from century to century under the guidance of a personal God, one and only, holy and eternal, who makes his divine assistance tangibly felt. He is so close to the people that he shows by signs and wonders his presence, his will and his word, his fatherly, strong and merciful rule; he is a God ready to punish transgressions of the Law he promulgated with authority (I am the Lord), but always patient and ready to forgive, to show mercy, to forget ingratitude (cf. Exod 34:6-9).

Israel feels its God as an omnipresent, superior, mighty and loving person. The history of the people is therefore an extraordinary history. No people and no nation in the world has ever felt so tangibly the fatherly assistance and effective presence of God as Israel did (Deut 32:7-14; Lev 26:44-45). It is a supremely educating presence, as shown by the explicit and repeated pledge that salvation would come from that very nation.

This is the first and only reason for the hope solemnly sealed by the covenant with Abraham (Gen 12:1-7; 15:1-18; 22:15-18), with the Patriarchs (Gen 28:10-22), with Moses (Exod 19-20) and with David, from whose line will rise the star that will be God-with-us (2 Sam 7:5-16).

⟦p. 34⟧

God in person speaks to the Patriarchs, to Moses, to the Prophets, his spokesmen to the people. They will continue to proclaim the threats deserved by deviations and transgressions, the misfortunes that will not fail to follow from the people's repeated infidelity to the covenant. At the first sign of repentance, however, these threats will at once be repaired by an overflowing of new graces and new favours. The history of the covenant people thus unfolds as a story woven of divine pedagogy, which reaches a high point before and after the slavery in Egypt and the liberation from it. This pedagogy prepares the covenant people for the supreme event of history: the Incarnation and the Redemption.

This, then, is the teaching of the spiritual life, imparted by God to his people through the word, the scriptures and the practice of penance. He trains them to acknowledge him as the one and only God, to contemplate created things with gratitude, to respect and love their neighbour, to detach themselves from their own possessions, even to the supreme sacrifice of detachment from their homeland. With the homeland God takes from the people all they have, to give it back to them later in a new way and in greater abundance. It is the salutary exercise of poverty, a prelude to the poverty of the Messiah to come.

Tossed from one land to another, uprooted from its own territory and led into a foreign land, Israel is trained in detachment, in poverty lived and suffered, in serving rather than being served.

⟦p. 35⟧

It was indispensable that the chosen people should prefigure, in an effective and concrete way, the poverty, humility and obedience of the One whom the Prophets announced as the Servant of Yahweh (Isa 42:1-7; 49:1-26; 50:4-11; 52:13-15; 53:1-12). It was necessary that they prepare to receive the Redeemer in lowliness: the poverty of his birth, a poor life, contradiction, the servile condition of a poor family in the school of a humble, unknown carpenter (Luke 2:39-52). It was a hard school, difficult to learn, for an independent people who aspired to dominion and earthly triumphs.

The difficulty and stiff-neckedness in learning the lesson of divine Wisdom are rooted in human nature itself. And this will be the scandal of the people at the coming of the Messiah, with his birth and simple life, which in the end will breed contradiction and rejection, to the point of demanding his death.

Through his divine interventions and direct or indirect messages God imparts to his people the first elements of wisdom: the fear of him, the characteristic truth of the covenant people (Sir 2:15ff.; 7:29ff.).

Adam and Eve fall into sin because, among other things, they lack the fear of God, the beginning of wisdom and holiness. In instilling fear towards the Absolute Creator, the Lord did not in fact intend to rule by fear at all. The fear of God is indeed the first beginning of love. Before the infinite and absolute divine majesty one is afraid of offending it, of not responding to its love; one fears not loving it as it deserves. In the fear of God, therefore, lies the first beginning of that love of God which will be the substance of the new Covenant.

⟦p. 36⟧

The pedagogy of divine wisdom is the effective call to fear the Lord; it is a warning that keeps alive hope, the sovereign virtue contained in the covenant whose substance is the great promise of the future Redeemer. A promise founded on faith in God's word, faith in the Word and promise of God, which places the virtue of hope at the centre of all the other virtues. One cannot have hope without faith in God's merciful omnipotence and without the support of his love for man, whom he created and placed at the summit of the visible created world. If the beginning of wisdom is the fear of God, this means it is a fear that is not an end in itself but preparatory, one that disposes to the love of God in all its fullness, made up of the infinite loveliness of the Creator and of the future Redeemer, the Teacher by essence in wisdom, love and holiness.

1.2. The people of the Covenant

⟦p. 37⟧

God, who reveals himself again and again in the history of Israel as One and Only, Holy and Eternal Living One, near, present and at work in the community of the chosen people, who reveals himself to individuals such as the Patriarchs, Moses and the Prophets, creates in the soul of whoever listens to him and remains faithful to him the expectation of the fulfilment of the divine promise: the joyful event of the incarnate Word, the promised God-with-us (Isa 7:14). This expectation lasts for centuries upon centuries, and as it lasts it grows more intense, more holily heart-rending, as can clearly be seen in the words of blessing of the holy old man Simeon when he has the joy of receiving Jesus in his arms, tired and weakened by ceaseless, suffering prayer, the fruit of a long wait: “Now, Lord, let your servant rest in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation, a light for the nations and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2:29-32). Yes, the deep, universal prayer that bursts from the depths of the hearts of the covenant people can be summed up in a few words: “Come, Lord Jesus!”.

It is the prayer proper to and characteristic of hope, the virtue that contains and defines the spirituality of Israel. The resounding miracle of the crossing of the Red Sea and the exceptional wonders God worked to free his people from slavery in Egypt prophetically magnified the hope of another, still more wonderful passage, the astonishment of heaven and earth: the expectation of the Man who would also be God.

Thus the true passage took shape: from the slavery of sin and its consequences to entry into the promised land of divinisation in Christ; from a mortal life, subject to the miseries and unhappiness of sin, to the eternal and immortal life of grace, through the more than wondrous grafting of limited and troubled human life into divine and eternal life, by virtue of grace!

⟦p. 38⟧

The hard-won spiritual wisdom of detachment from the world (from the treacherous land that holds the soul captive with its alluring and empty flatteries, far from the promised land of salvation) is truly a passage from extreme poverty, not only of material goods but above all the poverty of weakness and frailty in spiritual life, to the infinite riches of life in Christ.

The material poverty to which the covenant people is subject is a prophecy and a reminder of the nothingness of the creature and the all of God and his grace (cf. Ps 25:9; 9:19). In this sense poverty contains the sum of all the virtues, beginning with humility, with the lively sense of one's own nothingness, of one's native insufficiencies worsened by original sin, and of one's frailty before the mercy and the infinite, generous riches of God's goodness, which sets no limits to its gifts so as to restore to the human person the riches granted in the act of creation. These gifts, wonderfully increased, are guaranteed and made accessible by the grace of the head of the mystical body: Jesus Christ.

It is easy to understand, then, how this long wait for the Messiah was felt most keenly by those poor in material goods, tried by poverty and by the misfortunes of slavery, exile, the loss of their homeland, of their men and of all well-being.

These experiences gave rise to the small and poor “remnant of Israel”, which thus learned to live in faithfulness to the demands of Revelation, awaiting the fulfilment of the Lord's promises. These were precisely the conditions willed by the God of the Covenant so that the goodness of the redeeming God might shine out more clearly, even surpassing the goodness of God the creator.

⟦p. 39⟧

If we now wish to sum up in a few words the explicit and implicit, outward and inward prayer of the people of the Covenant, marked by hope, enlivened by faith and by grateful love for God, we can certainly identify it in the sigh of every soul that lives in the atmosphere of the covenant: “Come and save your people, come, O Redeemer God! Tear apart the shadow of waiting, come and free them from the slavery of sin, come, O almighty and merciful God!”

1.3. Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate

Saint Anne belongs to the people of the Covenant and in particular to the “little remnant”, a truth that can be deduced from God's own promise:

“Then those who feared God spoke with one another… The Lord gave ear and heard them… They shall become… my own possession on the day that I am preparing… For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven. Then all the proud and all who do wrong will be like straw… but for you who revere my name the sun of justice will rise with healing rays…” (Mal 3:16-20).

If she saw the sun of justice rise in her house, there is no doubt that Saint Anne lived the waiting, made of hope, of faith, of full trust in the promises of the Most High, with such inner ardour that she merited the grace of being chosen as mother of the Immaculate, the dawn of the Redemption, the pledge of the divine promises:

⟦p. 40⟧

“A shoot shall come forth from the stump of Jesse,

a branch shall grow out of his roots.

Upon him shall rest the spirit of the Lord,

a spirit of wisdom and understanding,

a spirit of counsel and might,

a spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord…

On that day

the root of Jesse

shall stand as a banner for the peoples…

His dwelling shall be glorious” (Isa 11:1-2.10ff.).

We can therefore attribute to Saint Anne the features of the authentic “poor one of God”, in the deepest sense of the word: a humble, simple, devout, poor person, yet rich in goodness, in charity, in such piety as to sum up in herself the aspirations of Israel, of the history and mission of the whole people of the Covenant, becoming an instrument of the fulfilment of the messianic promises, a firm bond of union and continuity between the old and the new Covenant, a sign of the goodness of God the Father, the infinite and primary source of all fatherhood and all motherhood.

No doubt Saint Anne spent her days in humility, in poverty, in daily work and above all in prayer centred on the fulfilment of the awaited Promises, and in charity towards her neighbour.

⟦p. 41⟧

How could the holy mother of the Immaculate have practised this whole rich heritage of virtues – poverty, humility, charity, piety – if she had not continually lived in all its fullness the principle God himself placed at the base of the whole spirituality of messianic expectation, the principle that founds and supports every other virtue like a cornerstone? It is, in practice, the principle God himself revealed to Abraham at the very moment he made the Covenant with him, as if offering “the Father of our faith” a means of the very highest value for remaining faithful to the Pact: “Walk before me and be perfect” (Gen 17:1). Here lies the substance of the spirituality of the old Covenant. Saint Anne practised this principle in the most perfect way; she walked in the presence of God, and when one walks continually before the gaze of God, who reads the depths of the soul, one walks towards holiness and an ever greater perfection. In this sense Saint Anne too grew day by day in holiness until she was ready for the extraordinary mission God would entrust to her. It was this uncommon holiness that made her the worthy mother of the Immaculate and a perfect anticipated model of the holiness lived and preached by Jesus. In this sense she is not only a high point of the holiness and spiritual perfection of the old Covenant, but a concrete foretaste of the spiritual perfection lived and preached by Jesus.

The bond between the holiness of the mother of the Immaculate and that of the new Covenant lies entirely here.

⟦p. 42⟧

Saint Anne therefore lived a solid and prayerful faith, filled with hope as she awaited the day of the Lord: come, come, O blessed Messiah, come to save and redeem your people, come, O desired of the nations, who chose Israel as your chosen people and as it were your favourite son. Come and soothe our aching longing for your tangible and beneficent presence. Come and light our way with word and deed (cf. Rule of 1869, p. 14).

God answered the prayer of his most faithful servant in a wondrous way, choosing her for a unique mission in the history of salvation, the mission of mother of the Immaculate, mother of the Mother of God. In her, therefore, the expectation of the old Covenant is fulfilled, and the radiant dawn of the new Covenant begins to shine.

In the order of divine Providence God grants special graces to those he calls to a particular mission in the work of Redemption.

If Saint Anne was called by God to be the mother of the Immaculate – the Mother of his divine Son – we may surely believe, resting on grounds of great fittingness, that she received uncommon mystical illuminations and communications, even though the Gospels are silent on this point. The inference, however, is anything but gratuitous. It would not be hard to appeal to highly probable theological arguments. Besides, a life lived continually according to the commandment God gave to Abraham, “Walk in my presence and you will be perfect…”, undoubtedly leads the soul to the high degrees of mysticism.

⟦p. 43⟧

Jesus' answer to the woman who, raising her voice from the crowd, had proclaimed blessed the womb that bore him and the breasts that nursed him, could not be understood otherwise: “blessed rather is the one who does the will of my Father in heaven”. Saint Anne certainly lived with unequalled fullness the command of divine perfection according to the old Covenant: “Walk before me. That is your perfection.” One cannot imagine that she did not fulfil perfectly the will of the Lord, the summit of perfection and the seal of all holiness, so much so that, had someone cried out to Jesus, “Happy the mother of the Immaculate, your Mother”, he would certainly have given an answer very like the one just recalled.

1.4. Mary, Daughter of Saint Anne, stands out among the humble and the poor who await the Lord

Saint Anne, the mother of the Immaculate, can also sing with her daughter Mary the Magnificat of thanksgiving. She is the mother of the One who incomparably surpasses the holiness of all creatures of heaven and earth, angelic and human, of the One greeted by the Archangel in the name of God the Father: “Full of grace, the Lord is with you!” Full of grace, yes! Full of grace as no other creature, angelic or human! The Lord is with you as with no other creature. One cannot imagine a creature holier than Mary, who reaches the very borders of the divinity, as the holy Fathers say. Such had to be the Mother of the incarnate Word, of the humanity of Christ, personally united to his divinity.

⟦p. 44⟧

Mary Most Holy not only stands out among the humble, the poor, the Saints who await the Lord, but, associated with Christ her son, she gives full meaning to the promises: the ransom and the coming of the Messiah, who takes upon himself the sin of humanity: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your offspring and hers; he will crush your head and you will lie in wait for his heel” (Gen 3:15). Here she is foreshadowed in the symbolic figure of the Daughter of Zion, which designates the people of God in what it has and keeps most pure and genuine. The Prophets greeted her in advance with psalms of joy and sorrow announcing the visit of the Lord, the fulfilment of the promises, the ransom, the imminent coming of the Messiah, who takes on himself the sin of humanity and associates her with himself in the mission that liberates and creates a new humanity. Raised to the dignity of Mother of God, Mary shares in the perfections of God in a way immensely superior to any other creature. In her every choicest virtue and every heavenly gift is concentrated, to gladden the angels, the saints and God himself.

In her the faith and hope of the Patriarchs and the Prophets are personified. Not for nothing does the Church greet her: “Our Hope”, hail!

She clearly stands out among the humble, the poor, among those who love God and neighbour, and above those most faithful to God's will, and she transcends beyond words in a splendour of holiness which, after the vision of God, makes the vision of her holiness a kind of second Paradise.

Mary is the Redeemer's collaborator in the work of redemption, sharing in his passion; she is the Sorrowful Mother par excellence because she is Immaculate, the shining star of the new Covenant, the Daughter of Anne who

⟦p. 45⟧

reflects upon the Mother the rays of her eminent holiness.

The Church greets the birth of Mary Most Holy from her holy mother Anne with the wonderful invocation: “Your birth, O Mary, is a proclamation of joy to the whole world!” (cf. Liturgical Office of the feast of the Nativity of Mary Most Holy).

Many are the passages of the books and the figures of the old Covenant that foreshadow, explicitly or implicitly, the holiness and almost more-than-creaturely mission of Mary Most Holy. There is, however, a passage of the Book of Proverbs that describes the work of creation. Reviewing the various stages of creation, the inspired Author states that the Creator “finds his delight in being with the children of men” (Prov 8:31).

How can this expression be understood, since it concerns the whole of human history and the whole people of the old and the new Covenant? How is it possible that God finds his delight in being with the children of men in this valley of evils and tears? There is an explanation! Beyond all sinners and rebels against God there is a creature in whom God, after the most holy humanity of the Word, finds his good pleasure: Mary Most Holy, the Immaculate, in whom all the virtues shine brightly: those announced and those preached by Jesus in the discourse of the beatitudes, and those he practised by his life and example.

Yes, the eye of God finds his delight in seeing the splendour of every virtue in Mary, Mother of Christ and of mankind. By reflection God sees humanity through the virtues and lofty holiness of Mary, who so greatly honours him

⟦p. 46⟧

and renders to him eternally, with her perfect adoration, her unspeakable love and her eminent holiness. Only by seeing humanity in the light of Mary Most Holy is God appeased and does he forgive the terrible ingratitude, the offences, the malice of poor, rebellious and sinful humanity. Thanks to her, God continues to find his delight in humanity, on which he continues to bestow his holiness, forgiveness and mercy.

the new Covenant, our only Hope

2.1. The Word made flesh in the womb of Mary, the handmaid of the Lord

The wonder of the holiness of Mary Most Holy, of the glory she gives to God, of the delight that through her pours out upon all humanity, takes on substance and value because Mary is intimately associated with the mediating and redeeming work of Christ, in whom the new Covenant is fulfilled, not only a relationship between God and man but an indissoluble bond uniting the two natures in the one person of Christ.

Humanity is taken up into the divine nature of the eternal Word of God. In the divine Redeemer the fullness of the divinity and the fullness of humanity are joined together, fulfilling in an immensely stronger way God's Covenant with humanity, a relationship of mutual friendship between God and the people of Israel.

⟦p. 47⟧

The Son of God, taking human nature, while remaining God and being from eternity one nature with the Father, becomes truly Man without confusion and without separation. The two natures constitute one divine Person. Here is the new Covenant, which is the incarnation of the Word, Jesus Christ himself.

Christ became “poor” in a divinely profound sense. The idea of “poverty” cannot therefore be limited to mere economic poverty, because then Jesus would simply be an exemplary model to imitate, while the true mystery of Christ, which is the incarnation and the redemption, would be left out. Christ's poverty certainly also refers to material poverty: he is born in a poor cave, has a poor manger for a bed, is wrapped in poor swaddling clothes by his most holy Mother… aspects that give exceptional prominence to the material poverty he chose; but, as already said, his poverty is of a divinely profound order.

2.2. Jesus, meek and humble of heart, in the mystery of his passion, death and resurrection

⟦p. 48⟧

According to Saint Paul, Jesus' poverty is expressed theologically in the fact that the Son of God, Lord, creator and king of the universe as he was, “though he was God, emptied himself, took the form and condition of a Servant, assuming human nature in the unity of the divine Person of the Word”. He becomes a “servant”! Compared with the divine nature, then, human nature is nothing. Though he was God, the absolute fullness of every good and every perfection, by uniting human nature personally to himself he lowered himself to the poverty of nothingness. He, the creator and master of all, made himself poor with the poverty of a servant (cf. Phil 2:7).

This supreme humiliation also includes the poverty of Mary, that of the family of Saint Anne and Saint Joachim, and the humiliation he accepted in becoming flesh in the most pure womb of the Immaculate, his Mother.

Jesus accepted the hardships of poverty during the thirty years of hidden and laborious life in Joseph's workshop, working as a carpenter; he lived the poverty of obscurity: “Is not this the carpenter's son?” (Matt 13:55); and in the three years of his public life he openly declared: “Foxes have the safety and warmth of their dens, birds their nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head!” (Matt 8:20; Luke 9:58). Jesus' poverty, therefore, has not only an economic meaning but a deep theological and spiritual one: God becoming a creature by taking the form of a “servant”; to come close to us God becomes one of us, in a gesture of infinite love, and finally lets himself be arrested, condemned to death, scourged, crowned with thorns, crucified and even stripped of everything, dying naked on the cross.

How else could the charism of Mother Rosa Gattorno, so deeply in love with the Crucified, be explained without this theological, ascetical and mystical background that so strikingly marks her life?

⟦p. 49⟧

2.3. Christ Jesus, priest and victim of the new and eternal Covenant

Jesus' poverty is also full, absolute, total acceptance of and adherence to the Father's will, so that he may be not only the Mediator (here is the new personal Covenant between God and man), but the Redeemer who takes upon himself the sins of all people and, through his sorrowful passion, death and resurrection, wins full victory over sin, hell and death. In this way he restores to man in overflowing measure the divine life of grace, becoming, through his luminous teaching and still more through his example, the light of the world for all humanity (John 8:12). Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word, is truly the new Covenant in the strong sense: God and man are in him one Person, the Mediator by essence between God and man, at once priest and victim, the one who makes reparation for all the faults and failures of humanity. He is the first, inexhaustible source, the firmest rock of hope for all humanity, the liberator from the prince of this world (the devil), the guarantor of salvation and eternal life, and the source of a hope immensely deeper than that of the Old Testament, a hope that will never fail because it is bound to him.

2.4. Christ Jesus, Lord of the Universe, will return in glory at the end of time

⟦p. 50⟧

The divine-human person of Christ Jesus will one day return in glory to judge humanity. That is why all humanity looks to him and awaits him trustingly, for an eternal life, a kind of deification of man, who in the most wonderful way becomes a sharer and partner in the infinite, eternal, most blessed life of God, a foretaste and an assurance for all who live in this hope.

It therefore seems fitting to recall here the expectation and hope of the old Covenant. As a whole, prophetic and foreshadowing the new Covenant, which is marked by the most lofty desire and joyful expectation of meeting Jesus in glory, the ancient inner cry of prayer, “Come, Lord Jesus!”, takes on new vigour, meaning, substance and ardour. It is a foretaste of Paradise. “Come, Lord Jesus!”, not only in human form but in the splendour of glory. Ultimately Jesus is the first and the last word: the first, implicit in the Promise; the last, explicit, that of the last of the sacred Books, the Apocalypse. Every soul awaits him, even if it lives among the appearances of a passing world, even if it seeks him where he is not, even when it rejects him because it does not know him.

With inspired and brilliant insight Mother Rosa raised the banner of hope as her programme and her charism.

⟦p. 51⟧

The hope poured into us by the Spirit, sent by Jesus to all his followers, awakens in us an unquenchable desire to see God face to face. With unutterable groanings the Holy Spirit pours into us a lively and growing longing to see God. What the Psalm says is thus wholly fulfilled: “My soul thirsts for the living God: when shall I come and see the face of God?” (Ps 42:3). And what does the soul seek, then, if not to see your Face? This is the unanimous sigh of the old and the new Covenant.

Mother Rosa contemplated the face of the Father mystically several times. With this light in her soul she saw clearly that the Father's face becomes present in the face of the Crucified Son, beloved, guide, well-beloved, Eucharist, that divine face that appeared visibly in Jesus, the incarnate Word.

To seek the face of God! In this inborn sigh of the soul, the image of God, the spirituality of the old and the new Covenant are wonderfully joined.

2.5. Christ Jesus associates Mary with his mystery of redemption

Closely and indissolubly associated with the work of redemption “as the generous companion and altogether exceptional cooperator of her Redeemer Son” (cf. LG 61), Mary Most Holy, the humble handmaid of the Lord wholly offered to the person and work of Christ, is under him and with him at the service of the mystery of redemption, becoming a cause of salvation.

What a wonderful opening to hope, then, is the mother of God and our mother!

⟦p. 52⟧

God willed to reach us through the powerful mediation and motherly help of Mary.

Mother Rosa clearly grasps this precise identity and Mary's lofty mission in God's saving plan. That is why, by calling the members of her spiritual Family “Daughters” [and Sons] of Saint Anne, she simply places at the centre the motherly role of Mary Most Holy, since the presence of Saint Anne clearly points to the wondrous power and greatness of her Daughter, Immaculate and most holy, proclaimed our mother by Jesus on Calvary, established for ever as mediatrix with the Mediator (cf. God's Gift…, pp. 137-138; 142-143), the Mother par excellence of all humanity.

In this sense we can well understand why God willed that all graces should come to us through Mary's hands.

2.6. Christ Jesus, one with the Father and the Holy Spirit

“I am in the Father and the Father is in me… if anyone loves me he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him… the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things…” (John 14).

Jesus reveals to us the inner life of God: One in three equal and distinct persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Mother Rosa, by a particular mystical gift of God, is admitted to contemplate this Trinitarian mystery and, made able to understand it, describes the experience with the depth God himself willed:

⟦p. 53⟧

“Great beyond all telling is the Most Holy Triad, infinite in God alone, infinite in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Equal in unity, perfect in Trinity. God alone, as one person alone, is seen, and at once in Jesus and in the Holy Spirit. In beholding the excellence and exquisiteness of these three Persons, in whom one always recognises one person, and three, without their being divided! My Love!” (M. 1.2, p. 1; cf. God's Gift…, pp. 32-33).

The Christian spiritual life is therefore profoundly Trinitarian. Every prayer, every liturgical act, every holy work begins in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The Most Holy Trinity is the first source and the final seal of Christian prayer, action and spiritual life. In this sense Christian hope too is a Trinitarian hope, a hope of progress in grace and of total victory over our faults and imperfections, even the smallest.

God, as a communion of persons, is therefore the foundation of our life, so that it may be an expression of concrete love in the service of humanity.

The burning thirst to share with Jesus, the victim of the new Covenant, God's plan and to carry it out in the Church in the dimension of love and communion shines through strikingly in Rosa Gattorno's spiritual journey: in her teachings, in the Constitutions and in the present Statutes of her charismatic family.

⟦p. 54⟧

3.1. A people journeying in hope,

awaiting the glorious manifestation of Christ

The hope that the people chosen by God in the Old Testament lived in the pact of Covenant God made with the Patriarchs, with Moses and the Prophets, was founded on the word of God. Hope, the banner of Mother Rosa's spirituality, is founded on the living and unshakeable rock that is Jesus Christ himself.

The people of the new covenant, the Church begotten by the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, journeys in hope, awaiting the final and glorious manifestation of Christ.

The presence between heaven and earth of an eternal high priest, the incarnate Word, cannot fail to affect humanity. Humanity, conformed anew to its Head through redemptive suffering and consecrated anew to the Father by the glory of the Son of Man, constitutes the Church, which is certainly the people of God, but also the new Eve born from the side of the new Adam, asleep on the cross in the sleep of a death that overcomes death for ever.

3.2. The Church, the body of Christ, enriched by the Holy Spirit with a variety of gifts and charisms

⟦p. 55⟧

The Church, like Christ himself, is a “mystery”, that is, a manifestation of God who gives himself to the creature. She is the very mystery of the glory of Jesus, taken in the broad, “earthly” sense, but including also the heavenly Church, a wonderful reality like all the works of God.

For these reasons we cannot enter into the knowledge and love of the Son of God who died and rose again except through the knowledge and love of the Church. We must, however, distinguish the Church as the mystical body of Christ, enriched with the Holy Spirit, the trustee of the treasures of grace and holiness merited by Jesus Christ, through which she has become his immaculate Bride, called to proclaim Christ to the world and endowed with a prophetic, priestly and kingly spirit, from her other aspects, which might obscure her reality.1 To distinguish, then, is to “clarify”.

A reality that shares in the mystery and holiness of God demands great precision and caution in language. The concept of the Church briefly sketched here, however, casts no shadow on the holiness of the Church herself.

Just as in the old Covenant God willed the most careful construction of the ark, as a tangible expression of the holy and sanctifying divine presence, so Jesus Christ founded the Church as the visible point of reference of his holy and sanctifying presence on earth for the salvation and redemption of mankind, rich in all the gifts and charisms of the Holy Spirit.

The Church we proclaim holy in the Creed with regard to the people who belong to her, who are not holy but called to holiness: it is wise to distinguish her clearly from the holy and sanctifying Church, the icon of the Most Holy Trinity.

To the Church so understood, that is, holy, sinners who persist in remaining cut off from Jesus Christ by sin do not belong. They belong to her only virtually, that is, to the extent that they repent and wish to return to Christ and live in the bosom of the Church. The Church and Christ, in fact, cannot be sharply separated.

3.3. A holy and sinful people called to holiness

The Church is truly the “people of God” to the extent that the baptised belong to Christ Jesus, to his mystical body. Precisely because the Church is identified with the “mystery hidden for ages in God”, which is Jesus Christ, the reality of the Church, like that of Jesus, is the work of divine wisdom, and is therefore immensely beyond our poor human concepts and our capacity to understand.

The Church is not only the “saved” people, the communion of believers, but also the “saving” universe.

⟦p. 57⟧

Like Mary, the Church too begets people to a new and immortal life: this is her motherhood in the Holy Spirit (cf. RM 44). To suppose that the sinner as such belongs to her formally, and not virtually, inclines one to think the Church sinful, in full contrast with the “holy” Church. Not for nothing is she a mystery! The Church, born of Christ's redeeming sacrifice and of the gift of the Holy Spirit, grafts us into Christ through the rite of baptism. Baptism has always been the outward expression of faith, of incorporation and of conversion, that is, of the firm decision to renounce the past and sin by radically changing one's mentality. Only on this condition does one become part of the people of God.

The image of the Church as the “people of God” must not therefore be isolated from the image of the Church as the mystical body and immaculate bride of Christ, as indeed the Council does not isolate it.

The Church as mystical body is a word inspired by the Holy Spirit; so Saint Paul proclaims it, and after him Tradition and the doctors of the Church, in particular Saint Augustine.

Only the image of the Church as mystical body allows us to understand that to break away (through sin) from the Head is to break away from the body, which is the members. In this sense whoever breaks away from the Head breaks away from the members.

⟦p. 58⟧

The image of the Church as the “people of God” has the advantage of throwing the door wide open also to those who belong to her only virtually, because all people, just as they are called to Jesus Christ, head and king of humanity, are called to the Church. In this sense those too who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel and the Church, but live honestly, belong to the soul, though not to the body, of the Church. And if they live honestly according to the natural moral law written by God in their hearts, the Lord will not fail to come to their aid and save them at the hour of death. This truth, however, must not quench the missionary zeal Jesus kindled on earth: “go and preach the Gospel to every creature”. Who can ever reckon the advantage of those who have the grace to live united to Jesus and his immaculate Bride, and the disadvantage of being outside? “I came to bring fire on the earth, and what do I wish but that this fire of truth, love and peace be kindled more and more?” (Luke 12:49).

Not for nothing is the Church a “mystery”, and the study of her characteristics fills one of the most fascinating treatises of Theology.

3.4. A prophetic, priestly and kingly people sent to proclaim the Kingdom

Christ, the great prophet, who by the witness of his life and the power of his word proclaimed the kingdom of the Father, fulfils his prophetic office until the full manifestation of his glory (LG 35).

⟦p. 59⟧

In him all the faithful, made sharers in his mystical body through the outpouring of his Holy Spirit, form a holy and royal priesthood, offer spiritual sacrifices to God through him and proclaim the greatness of him who called them out of darkness into his marvellous light.

There is therefore no member of the Church who has no part in the mission of the whole body; each must sanctify Jesus in his heart and bear witness to him in a spirit of prophecy (cf. PO 2), so that the power of the Gospel may shine forth.

The Church is truly a prophetic, priestly and kingly people, not only through baptism but also through the Eucharist, in which Jesus exercises his eternal priesthood, which is at once sacrifice and sacrament. The sacrifice of the Mass is the same sacrifice as that of the cross.

In the Eucharist Jesus, the eternal priest, continues to immolate himself mystically, to exercise his priesthood as head of the Church, his mystical body.

Baptism, which makes the Christian holy because it confers sanctifying grace, lays the foundations of Christian perfection and makes the baptised a sharer in Jesus' priesthood and prophetic power.

The members of Mother Rosa's charismatic Family, committing themselves to live their baptism intensely, grow in the prophetic dimension that reveals the saving and merciful love of God, and cooperate with all their strength in the spread and growth of Christ's Kingdom in the world, serving Christ in others and leading all their brothers and sisters to him with humility and patience (cf. LG 35; 36).

⟦p. 60⟧

3.5. Mary, Mother of the Church,

image of the new Jerusalem

Mary holds in the Church the highest place and the one closest to Christ. She is the image and beginning of the Church and is united to the Church through her union with the Redeemer.

Associated with the saving mystery of the Son and now glorified in heaven in body and soul – the first fruits of the Church, which will reach its definitive fulfilment in the age to come – Mary shines on earth as a sign of future hope and consolation (cf. LG 68), pointing out the way to follow.

Her motherhood, begun at the annunciation and sustained without wavering beneath the cross, “therefore lasts without interruption until the eternal fulfilment of all the elect” (cf. LG 61; 62), so that the Father's plan of salvation inaugurated by Christ may be accomplished.

The baptised who take part in the Eucharist find themselves in the same situation as Mary at the foot of the cross and offer God the Father the unbloody sacrifice, which has the same redemptive value as Jesus' bloody sacrifice: the Sacrifice of the new and eternal Covenant.

There is no more powerful sign of belonging to the Church, the people of God, than taking part in the Eucharist. That is why Mother Rosa let herself be radically drawn in by Jesus present in this Sacrament.

⟦p. 61⟧

And like her, her spiritual sons and daughters, living a strong sense of belonging to the Church, place the Eucharist at the centre of their lives and seek to take part in it daily, learning from Mary to contemplate Christ Jesus, Victim and Priest of the new Covenant, and to identify with him, mindful that the holy mother Anne too lived the same mystery in figure and awaited its full unveiling.

Compared with the old, the new Covenant is the masterpiece of the Most Holy Trinity, because it is fulfilled through the incarnation of the Word.

If the old Covenant was grace, the choice of a people, divine assistance, God's fatherly and teaching presence, the new Covenant is the hypostatic and personal union of God with man, as vast as the bounds of humanity.

Since the new Covenant is Jesus Christ himself, besides faithfulness charity is needed, clearly included in the hope of meeting the glorious Jesus Christ in the light of the Most Holy Trinity, the life of the angels and the blessed in heaven.

The new Covenant must be lived, precisely by virtue of hope. This means living Jesus Christ crucified on earth, generously accepting the trials and sufferings by which we prepare ourselves to meet him in glory.

⟦p. 66⟧

On this point nothing is more eloquent than the life and example of Mother Rosa, a lofty and inspiring model for all who generously embrace her charism and wish to live the virtues she lived with heroic ardour all her life.

1.1. Faith: loving adherence to the God of the Covenant, Father, Son and Holy Spirit

Faith makes us believe firmly in the word of God, of which Abraham (Gen 15:6) gave heroic proof, ready for the gravest of sacrifices, wholly abandoned to God's infinite merciful goodness.

No less was Moses' full and trusting abandonment to God on so many occasions during the long and troubled pilgrimage towards the promised land. His faith is such that it turns into complete confidence and trust, to the point of halting the threats of God, rightly angered by the people's many infidelities. This faith, resting entirely on the promise of the future Redeemer, is the prelude to Christian faith, not only in Jesus Christ as Messiah, but essentially as God, identical with the Father, under the veils of human flesh, as today under the veils of bread and wine.

The key point of Christian faith, then, is to believe in the divinity of Christ, proclaimed by John in the Prologue of his Gospel and explicitly confirmed by Jesus himself more than once: “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58).

⟦p. 67⟧

The clear witness to his divinity will indeed be the decisive reason for his condemnation to death by crucifixion. To the high priest who asks him, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God”, Jesus replies, “You have said so yourself.” Then Caiaphas tears his garments, saying, “He has blasphemed! What further need have we of witnesses?” And the whole Sanhedrin decrees, “He deserves death” (Matt 26:62ff.). Jesus bears open witness to his divinity. Before this witness the death sentence follows at once: “He called himself Son of God. We need no more witnesses.”

All those present were witnesses of what he testified about himself; yet only some who were truly just and sincere, like Nicodemus, would become his followers.

The first and principal truth of faith is therefore the divinity of Christ, from which all the others spring: faith in the Most Holy Trinity, the truth of all the mysteries of Christ: resurrection, ascension, descent of the Holy Spirit, including the divine motherhood of Mary Most Holy.

This is the faith we must ask for in every prayer, as the Apostles asked Jesus: “We believe, Lord, but increase our faith!” (Luke 17:5).

⟦p. 68⟧

If Jesus Christ is Son of God and, as man, Son of Mary, Our Lady is not only mother of the Church but symbolises her most splendid icon, the living image of the Church's very mission. She was the First to believe that the Messiah would be “Son of God”, through the explicit revelation made to her by the archangel Gabriel: “He who will be born of you will be great and will be called Son of the Most High… and he will reign for ever over the house of Jacob” (Luke 1:32).

The dramatic exchange before the Sanhedrin and Mary's own wonder at the angel's greeting raise a serious question: the people of the old Covenant were certain that the Messiah would come. But did they know that the Messiah would be the Son of God? He would be a great king, a liberator, a redeemer; but would he be God himself incarnate in the person of the Word?

The fact is of such divinely exceptional greatness that when Peter declares, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”, Jesus answers him, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven” (cf. Matt 16:16-17).

With the mystery of the incarnation of the Word, who is God, the promises made to Abraham, to the Patriarchs, to Moses and to the Prophets take on extraordinary dimensions, beyond all poor human imagining. Even the prophecy that the Messiah would be Emmanuel could be understood in different ways. What God's omnipotence could accomplish, only the facts and Jesus' own open confession have revealed to us, giving us possession of this reality beyond all human imagining. That is why the basic virtue of faith in Christ's divinity is needed above all. Then faith becomes unconditional adherence to Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word: born in poverty and dying naked on the bare cross.

⟦p. 69⟧

This truth necessarily leads to total adherence to the supreme mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, the threefold ocean of infinite love into which the Word draws us while we are still pilgrims on earth.

For souls striving for perfection and arrived at the highest summits, like Mother Rosa, continually immersed in God, this adherence becomes total trust, an inner, familiar and uninterrupted dialogue.

The virtue of faith in God can and must grow day by day. That is why we must make our own the prayer the Apostles addressed to Jesus: “We believe, Lord, increase our faith!” (Luke 17:6). The increase of faith brings with it an increase of hope.

Faith, the foundation of what is hoped for, helps us to live, conforming our life to the teaching and example of Christ; it spurs us to welcome the Word of God with joyful devotion, makes us recognise God's will in daily life, and makes us see in events the signs of the times that show what God wants of us

Faith is always certainty because it rests unshakeably on the authority of God, an absolute certainty higher than all human certainties, and for that very reason founded on the full and exclusive authority of God, from which every human certainty, rational certainty included, springs.

Its value derives from the absolute infallibility of Christ, the incarnate Word, who willed to leave even on earth a living image of himself in the Pope, the “sweet Christ on earth”, who, assisted by the Holy Spirit, becomes the guardian and guarantor of revealed truths.

⟦p. 70⟧

The shining star of faith is Mary Most Holy, our model and our help in steadfastness in this virtue; we never turn to her without having already received, through her intercession, the spiritual graces needed for daily growth on this path of adherence to God. That is why we greet her: “Hail, our Hope!”.

No one ever had or will have such fullness and firmness of faith as Mary Most Holy.

This is the great grace she pours into our minds and hearts: a faith that is certainty of the fulfilment of God's promises, a joyful certainty that the Spirit is present and at work in the kingdom of God and leads us with absolute assurance to the final goal, despite the crosses and persecutions stirred up by the enemy of the human race, whose head she, the Immaculate, has victoriously crushed.

She is truly the Mother of faith, the victorious one par excellence. Her powerful motherly watchfulness guarantees that every obstacle in the way between the “already” and the “not yet” will be overcome, a way we are invited to walk with the greater serenity Mary teaches us by her sharing in the passion and glorious resurrection of her divine Son, who made her our mediatrix, advocate, helper and succour.

⟦p. 71⟧

Mary Most Holy is our perfect model and our powerful help in growing in faith, the most convincing proof of God's infinite fatherly and motherly tenderness. He willed her to be mediatrix with the Mediator, a sure guide on the tiring yet joyful way of our holiness. To pray to her is to pray to Jesus more effectively. To imitate her virtues is to imitate, as in a shining mirror, the virtues of Jesus.

Mary is the mother of our faith because we feel her close to us, especially when we take part in the sacrifice of the Mass. We feel her close because she has always intervened, and always intervenes, in the difficult moments of our life and of the Church herself, the body of Christ and people of God. More than once, at the gravest moments of history, she has intervened and still intervenes tangibly to encourage and help us, as if to assure us of victory despite all the snares and diabolical wiles unleashed by the enemy of the human race.
