She is the sure shield of our faith and of our spiritual life: “Our life, our sweetness and our hope!” At this point two reflections arise spontaneously: the faith of the old Covenant was founded on a promise of God, and God certainly does not promise in vain; the faith of the new Covenant is founded on the most astounding, though silent, work of God, who becomes Man and makes the union with human nature in the eternal Word the indissoluble seal of the Covenant, as the union of the divine nature with human nature is indissoluble; he also works the wonder of preserving the Mother from every stain of sin, since she is loved by the Father as no other creature.

⟦p. 72⟧

If in this horizon Mary was eternally present in the mystery of Christ, through the faith inherited from her holy mother Anne; she came, however, to share in it throughout the whole extent of her earthly journey (cf. RM 19).

What unshakeable divine support, then, our faith has, and consequently our hope! And the comparison arises spontaneously with the faith and hope of the Old Testament, only a pale figure of our present happy reality.

Saint Anne undoubtedly had most singular graces and privileges. Her mission in the plan of Redemption required it: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev 21:5; cf. Isa 43:19), and Saint Paul confirms: “With the Incarnation of the eternal Word all things have been made new” (2 Cor 5:17). But new and immensely stronger is our faith. Faith in the God of the Covenant did not disappoint the just of the Old, and does not and cannot disappoint the followers of Christ and of his Church. Of the chosen people only a “little remnant” had remained faithful, whose poverty of spirit is reflected in the poverty of Mary and Joseph. Even so, God does not fail his Word.

1.2. Hope in the God of the Covenant, who does not disappoint

Certainly this hope does not disappoint or confound, because its guarantor is God himself made Man. On these divinely unshakeable foundations “hope does not disappoint and cannot disappoint” (Rom 5:5).

Within the diminished people of Israel there is indeed a “little remnant”, the family of Saint Anne, on whom God could count.

⟦p. 73⟧

The great majority of the people, however, thought like the apostles themselves before the descent of the Holy Spirit. Jesus' closest friends in fact wondered which of them would be the greatest in the new kingdom now come, and the mother of the two brothers went so far as to ask Jesus for a privileged place for her sons. This was a purely human outlook, as we can see from Jesus' answer to Peter, who wanted to dissuade him from facing the passion and death: “Get behind me, Satan! Your language comes from human wisdom. You are thinking not as God does, but as men do” (Matt 16:23). His is a very harsh reply, unlike the language he ordinarily used.

Saint Anne, then, certainly merited to become the mother of Mary through her hope in the coming of the Messiah and his kingdom. Mary lived this same hope. Her lofty holiness gathered in herself all the hope of Israel and surpassed it to such a degree that God could no longer delay the fulfilment of his promises, choosing her to be the mother of the Messiah. With her the promise of the Covenant goes beyond the bounds of Israel and of history. Upon her rests the good pleasure of the Most Holy Trinity, so that she merits the most wonderful revelation of the reality of the awaited Messiah: “…he will be Son of God”.

Mary Most Holy also pours into our hearts a new kind of hope: the certainty that the Holy Spirit is working a “new creation”.

If the Messiah is the Son of God, hope acquires absolute certainty. All the prophecies and figures of the

⟦p. 74⟧

old Covenant take on a dazzling light: Mary becomes in the full sense the mother of hope, the one who will defeat the assaults the powers of hell plot against the Church and against souls seriously resolved to follow Jesus Christ to the summit of Calvary, as Mother Rosa so boldly did. Here is Christian hope! In Mary we have the sure shield of our faith and our hope. The daughters of Saint Anne, and all the other members of the Family of the holy mother of Mary Immaculate, are charismatically called to live Jesus our Hope, a feature that distinguishes their spirit and links it in a special way to the holiness of the mother of the Immaculate. This distinctive aspect of the spirituality of Mother Rosa's charismatic Family marks unmistakably the charism inherited from the Foundress, shaped by the spirituality of expectation lived by the mother of the Immaculate, and conforms it to the authentic, classic spirituality of the Catholic Church: “To live the Covenant in Christ Jesus, our hope”. Among the theological virtues, then, the virtue of hope stands out. This emphasis takes nothing away from the substance of Christian spirituality in every age, and characterises the charism well. One may say that the charismatic primacy of Hope gains an extra note compared with the spirituality of other religious Families, as though Mother Rosa's followers wished to superimpose on the expectation of the glorious Jesus the long and pregnant waiting of the chosen people, lived in all its fullness by Saint Anne and her most holy Daughter.

⟦p. 75⟧

The emphasis on the theological virtue of hope implies vigilance, the virtue Jesus urged most strongly: “Stay awake and pray, for the Son of Man will come at the hour you least expect”; “Watch and pray” (Matt 25:13). This is the attitude of those who abhor the great enemy of spiritual progress, which is lukewarmness, sloth and the spiritual sleep that blocks the way up to the summits of the interior life.

It was precisely this watchful and wary constancy in prayer that led Mother Rosa to the heights of holiness.

1.3. Charity, the fire of “divine Love”

Charity grows in those who hope, and by hoping they increase their faith day by day.

The charity of Christ makes both faith and hope alive and active. One may say that faith and hope are the virtues of the poor, also in the sense that one hopes for what one does not possess and believes what one does not see.

The path of salvation, however, is marked by the growth and development of the love of God.

“God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that whoever believes in him should not die but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

God is infinite Love; he created the world for love of us and redeemed it with a love still greater and more wonderful. Moreover, he declares that in the love of neighbour lies the full fulfilment of the law. Here is the vast and moving sense of poverty.

⟦p. 76⟧

Just as God the Father veiled his divinity in the Son within our humanity, so we must strip ourselves entirely of our innate selfishness in order to put on Jesus entirely (cf. Rom 13:10).

Love by its nature transforms. The more we love Jesus, the more we are transformed and identified with him. Poverty in the deepest sense of the word works this miracle: the stripping of self and identification with Christ. Charity is unconditional openness to boundless love for God, living as children loved by him in fraternal communion. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father (cf. John 14:21).

Charity towards God becomes a gift to one's neighbour, a sign of God's fatherly and motherly love for every creature.

The coming of the Kingdom takes place in each person to the extent that he or she loves Christ, because the Kingdom is Jesus Christ himself, and his coming in glory is accomplished to the extent that the person who believes in and loves God is filled with Jesus and identified with him.

Here lies the substance of the Christian spiritual life. Here lies the key to progress and growth in holiness: the universal vocation of whoever chooses Jesus Christ, Son of God, “the way, the truth and the life” (John 14:6).

⟦p. 77⟧

“Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I too will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:23). Of all the theological virtues, charity is the one that puts us in direct contact with God. “Charity, in a certain way, unlike every other virtue, unites directly to God” (Saint Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, III, Dist. 3, q.1). “All the goodness of the soul lies in charity” (S.Th. I Sent. Dist. 17, q.9, a.1). “Charity is the life of the soul; as the soul is closely and immediately united to the body, so charity unites immediately to God” (S.Th. II-II, q.23, a.2). “The charity with which we love our neighbour is a participation in divine charity” (Ibid. a.2 ad 2). “The virtue of charity with which one loves God, oneself (not selfishly) and one's neighbour is one and the same, just as the virtue of hope with which one hopes for oneself and for others is one and the same” (S.Th. II-II, q.17, a.3).

“So one may say that the love of God is hope in action, hope at work. The virtue of Charity (of the love of God) is the gift in which all the other gifts are given to the soul” (S.Th. III Dist. 9 q.1 a.1). “Charity is the principle of all the other virtues, just as prudence is the principle that unites and regulates all the moral virtues” (III Dist. 27, q.2, a.4). “Right and ordered love is included in every other virtue” (II-II, q.125, a.4).

We can well understand, then, Jesus' invitation: “Remain in my love and you will have every good” (John 15:9).

⟦p. 78⟧

Hope grows strong, great and deep on the foundation of faith, charity and the love of God, because it is not reduced to the slender thread of history! The old and the new Covenant are something far greater than history itself. The incarnation of the Word, the first and ineradicable foundation of the history of the Old and New Testaments, is the most astounding of God's works. All the saved have had, and now have, salvation thanks to the merits of Christ, of infinite and ever-present value, under the movement of the Holy Spirit, whether before the incarnation or after it, thanks to the passion and death of Jesus.

The work of creation, especially of the human person, is a wonderful work worthy of almighty God. Immensely greater is the work of redemption, so that the Church does not hesitate to declare: God was wonderful in creating human nature, but still more wonderful in restoring and reforming it through Jesus Christ.

The event of the two Covenants, old and new, must be placed in a metahistorical perspective, that is, above history and as the foundation of history, which is the work of Redemption.

Creation, on which all history is founded, is itself a metahistorical intervention of God. It is God who freely and gratuitously pours out ad extra (outside himself) the infinite fire of his love. The work of redemption therefore continues and expands, in the most wonderful way, truly worthy of God, his love for creatures, or rather for the masterpiece of creation, which is man.

The whole history of the old and the new Covenant is centred on the divine person of Jesus, Son of God and Son of Man, that is, son of the Virgin Mary, the Immaculate.

At the foundation of the history of salvation, therefore, lies God's love for the human person.

⟦p. 79⟧

Creation and redemption are therefore realities that go back to the love God has for the human creature, the first origin of all history, which finds in the incarnate Word its deepest meaning and its root.

In him and through him everything is explained and everything finds its reason and its one meeting point. We can well understand, then, the meaning of the words of Jesus' great prayer: “Holy Father, keep in unity all those you have given me, that they too may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you… so that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory you gave me I have given to them, that they may be one as we are one” (John 17:20-21). Here is the way of Christian perfection and holiness: to become one with Jesus, to identify progressively with him, so as to become one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Mother Rosa lived and taught the way to reach such holiness, longing as she did to become one with Christ crucified. To live hope, then, is to set it within love for the Crucified. Hence the living and perennial relevance of the charism of Mother Rosa, who could well say with Saint Paul: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor 2:2).

This was also Mother Rosa's (especially mystical) wisdom. But this wisdom is nothing other than the ardent love for Jesus and in particular for Jesus crucified, as can easily be deduced from the facts of her life and from her mystical writings. The love of God is in fact a source of light and wisdom, as Aquinas openly states: “The ardour of charity is changed into the light of

⟦p. 80⟧

knowledge and wisdom” (Commentary on the Gospel of Saint John, c. V).

Mother Rosa's life was so united to that of Jesus, particularly to Jesus crucified, that she could say with Saint Paul: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Gal 2:20); and again: “for me to live is Jesus Christ” (Phil 1:21). Mother Rosa's mystical experience reached these wonderful heights. At the root of the many mystical graces God granted her lay this painful, joyful and luminous identification with Jesus crucified. All the wealth of Mother Rosa's mystical graces (and they are many) flowers from this fundamental reality: love for Christ crucified, whom she calls “my Good”.

In the person of Jesus, therefore, the history of the old and the new Covenant finds its origin and foundation. Their unity is constituted by Jesus who was to come, Jesus who has come, Jesus who is coming. The old Covenant was the prelude and prophecy of what would be revealed and accomplished in the new Covenant, personified in Jesus Christ, Son of the Father and Son of Mary, through his example (Jesus teaches more by deeds than by words) and above all through the full adherence of his will to the Father's at the supreme moment of accepting the passion and death. The old Covenant then becomes a song of love for God and neighbour, the love practised and preached by Jesus Christ and already anticipated in many Psalms: “I love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps 18:2); “Love the Lord, all you his saints” (Ps 31:24).

⟦p. 81⟧

The fundamental law is no different from the one promulgated by Jesus, even though he perfected it divinely: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength” (Deut 6:5).

It is the work of salvation accomplished by God in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, in whom the long expectation of the One who would be the Saviour of all, and of those who would be faithful to the old as to the new Covenant, finds its fulfilment and meaning.

Within the people of God, in fact, some persons are particularly chosen and favoured by him for the special mission he entrusts to them. Among them our gaze rests on the family of Saints Joachim and Anne, the parents of Mary, chosen precisely for so lofty a mission.

For Rosa Gattorno's charismatic family, therefore, the supreme example of love of God and neighbour is Mary Most Holy, who, being Mother of God, is by that very fact mother of divine Love in its twofold dimension: vertical, towards God, and horizontal, towards neighbour, on the foundation of the humanity taken from her by the Word in the mystery of the incarnation.

1.4. Simplicity: “let everything in you be light”

Besides the life of faith, hope and love, the people of the Covenant live in transparency, as a demand of full acceptance and inner adherence to the word of God.

⟦p. 82⟧

Israel knew that whoever seeks God must flee all duplicity: neither persons nor things must divide his heart (Ps 119:130); no ambiguity must creep into his conduct and his words (Ps 119:10ff.).

Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate, and above all Mary personify the full maturity of the chosen people in the virtue of simplicity too. They are the visible expression of what Jesus teaches about this virtue: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is sound, your whole body is full of light; but if it is diseased, your body is in darkness. Take care, then, that the light in you is not darkness. If your whole body is full of light, with no part of it in darkness, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp lights you with its rays” (Luke 11:34-36).

Jesus was clearly speaking figuratively, adapting himself to the Eastern mentality of his hearers. The meaning of his words becomes clear for us too if we put “soul” in place of “body”, and in place of material light the light of the intellect and the spiritual transparency of our conscience. But when does our soul become full of light? The answer is certainly demanding. The soul is wholly luminous when it is free of all sin, indeed of every fault and every passion. Every fault and every passion not fully mastered darkens the soul, little or much.

⟦p. 83⟧

In the passage quoted Jesus seems clearly to demand total luminosity, that is, victory over and freedom from every fault and every inner resentment. This is the precondition of simplicity, as can be inferred from another saying of Jesus: “Truly I tell you, unless you turn and become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever becomes little like this child will be the greatest in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt 18:2-4).

Simplicity is the soul's luminosity when it is free of every form of self-centredness and lives habitually in serenity and inner peace, above all disturbance, because it rests in Jesus.

It is the simplicity typical of the saints, who let themselves be guided solely by right intention, ready to listen to and carry out the promptings of the Holy Spirit, always seeing God's will in obedience to legitimate superiors, free from any inner or outer resistance and from any ulterior motive dictated by self-love. Simplicity, contrary to the sound of the word, is a virtue rich in values and content, a virtue practised and held dear above all by Jesus and by Mary Most Holy. It makes whoever possesses it ready for every other virtue and every sacrifice.

Simplicity shuns every artifice and subterfuge, every lack of sincerity, every futile complaint, the smallest lie. In a word, simplicity implies victory over all purely human views in order to move in an entirely supernatural spirit. One might say that simplicity lived in the luminous fullness Jesus wills implies the attainment of total conversion to God; in a word, the attainment of holiness.

⟦p. 84⟧

From this we see how rich Mother Rosa's charism is, and also the magnificent inheritance she left to her whole spiritual Family.

“Little girls are extremely dear to Jesus; but do you know what kind of souls Jesus loves? Little ones, humble ones, who, because they are little, do not yet have that monster of self-love which is the property of the old man” (Letter to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, September 1870).

The virtue of simplicity wonderfully eases the love of God and neighbour. Without this virtue, which makes all spiritual activity luminous, hope founded on the love of God and neighbour cannot develop. With simplicity there enters the soul docility to the Word of God and openness to his invisible sanctifying action; there enter freedom in truth, rectitude of heart, transparency, harmony, authenticity of life, the overcoming of all duplicity in speaking with others, following Jesus' command: “Let your speech be yes, yes; no, no; anything more comes from the evil one” (Matt 5:37).

The virtue of simplicity, in the richness of its expressions, can become the subject of precious meditations.

1.5. Prudence: letting oneself be guided by Love

Simplicity and prudence form an inseparable pair.

⟦p. 85⟧

The chosen people knew the importance of letting themselves be prudently guided by God, by wisdom (cf. Wis 9:11); when unsure of a choice, they were called to respect the supreme dominion of God: “To God belong counsel and prudence” (Job 12:13). From generation to generation the faithful learned: “Learn prudence, you simple ones” (Prov 8:5); “wisdom teaches temperance and prudence” (Bar 3:9ff.).

Saint Anne and Mary her daughter had been educated in this school, enlightened by that prudence which Jesus would teach as Master to the whole of humanity.

When he sends his disciples to proclaim the Gospel, he warns them: “I send you out like sheep among wolves; so be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt 10:16).

Jesus' warning keeps all its value today, as it had in the time of Mother Rosa, who lived applying to all her choices the criteria of this virtue, never separating it from simplicity.

“Prudence is that light which, between two things, makes you always choose the one that better leads you to acquire and increase the love of God” (Rule 1869, p. 25).

No virtue stands, then, without prudence. Indeed the Christian and also pre-Christian moral tradition defines prudence as the virtue of virtues, the virtue that guides and directs all the others.

⟦p. 86⟧

A soul consecrated to God, generous, intelligent, hard-working, full of good will, eager for holiness, humble, pure, poor and docile, if it lacks prudence exposes all its other virtues to danger. And when the virtues are in danger, it is as if one did not have them.

A fine edifice of virtues without the safeguard of prudence is like the house built on sand of which Jesus speaks in the Gospel (cf. Matt 7:26).

Prudence, then, is the firm rock on which the edifice of the other virtues stands. It regulates, indeed perfects, all the moral virtues. This most important virtue guides the person in the sphere of action, in choosing what to do in order to reach Christian perfection and holiness. The very recent Constitutions take up, in a modern style and with great faithfulness and refinement, the teaching of the Rule of 1869:

“Simplicity, which ‘cannot live without the company of prudence’, forms with it an inseparable pair which, sincerely lived, leads to the possession of true wisdom… Christ is not only the Teacher who teaches the practice of this virtue: his very person is the foundation of Christian prudence, because he is the one and absolute criterion that enables us to discern and judge the various spirits…” (Const., art. 19).

⟦p. 87⟧

How fitting and wise it is to equate prudence with wisdom! The virtue of prudence practised according to the criteria of the Rule of 1869, and more concisely in the very recent edition approved by the Holy See, is a most valuable help for walking safely on the way of perfection.

1.6. Humility: “the way to the exaltation that comes from God”

Identification with the poor Christ, the true heart of the Institute's spirituality, finds its characteristic expression in humility, which is the pivot of Jesus' life and teaching: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt 11:29). This will be all the more broadly and deeply true if the expression “poor Jesus” is understood in the wide and strong sense, as Saint Paul says: “You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, he became poor for your sake, so that you might become rich through his poverty” (2 Cor 8:9). The Letter to the Philippians states the meaning of Jesus' poverty more strongly still: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a treasure to be jealously guarded, but emptied himself, taking the condition of a servant and becoming like men; appearing in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even to death on a cross. Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue proclaim that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Phil 2:6-11).

⟦p. 88⟧

In the light of Jesus, the daughters of Saint Anne and those called by Christ to imitate this distinctive attitude of his, choosing the last places, serving as he himself did with all gentleness and goodness, and working tirelessly for the spread of the Kingdom, aware that the gifts received are for the common upbuilding, must make their own the words of the Gospel: “When you have done all you were commanded, say: we are useless servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17:10), not aspiring to greatness but letting themselves be drawn by what is humble (cf. Rom 12:16).

Humility understood in this way widens the space of charity towards God and towards neighbour.

A soul dominated by self-love in all its many forms can neither love God nor serve its neighbour. The more sincere and deep humility is, the greater the charity in which perfection chiefly consists.

⟦p. 89⟧

How many times during the day we must ask the Lord to sweep from our soul and heart every feeling of selfishness, praying that he will come, ever more effectively, to take the place of our self. Let us not forget to heed Saint Paul's warning: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Cor 4:7). The gifts and endowments of nature and grace granted by God cannot be denied. What matters is not to boast of them, because every endowment and every good comes from him. The gifts received must therefore be welcomed with humble gratitude towards the Giver of every good, because the humble acknowledgement of the truth is the very substance of humility.

When this attitude towards God is in the heart, there follows the awareness of being sinners, but at the same time the certainty that God saves us.

Humility was the fundamental attitude of the “Remnant of Israel”, and undoubtedly that of Mary's holy parents, and of Mary, who lived it to the highest and most exemplary degree, being Immaculate, the humble spouse of the just Joseph and mother of Jesus, meek and humble of heart. That is why the daughters of Saint Anne, and all the members of the Family of the Holy mother of the Immaculate, regard humility as the foundational virtue of their spirituality, as Mother Rosa taught:

“Great prudence, charity, humility, gentleness with everyone… and you will win the hearts of all, to make them all the Lord's” (Letter to Sr. A. Agnese Tacchini, 1900).

1.7. Meekness: the spontaneous radiance of humility

It is one of the virtues Jesus urges us to practise in imitation of him: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt 11:29).

⟦p. 90⟧

Echoing the wealth of values expressed in the Rules of 1869, the new Constitutions sum up excellently the nature of this virtue, which Mother Rosa instilled in the souls of her daughters:

“I recommend to you… meekness, because this is the true character of a daughter of Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate” (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, 13/5/1872).

“Whenever you have to speak, do not think too anxiously about what you are to answer, but present yourself to anyone without any study except that of charity and gentleness, with simplicity…” (Threads of Gold, p. 159).

Meekness is the way Jesus chose to proclaim the Kingdom of God. This virtue, practised sincerely in everyday encounters, penetrates people's hearts and makes them open and receptive to the language of the Gospel, so that Christ's words come true: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt 5:5). The promise Jesus made to the meek was foreshadowed in the promise God made to Abraham and his descendants.

Psalm 37 contains a prophetic anticipation addressed explicitly to the meek, who are destined to inherit the earth. In practice the Psalm repeats what God had said to Abraham. Israel itself was called to enjoy the inheritance, on condition, however, that it remained faithful to the Covenant: “You shall do what is pleasing in the eyes of the Lord” (Deut 6:18). “The meek shall possess the earth and enjoy great peace” (Ps 37:11ff.).

⟦p. 91⟧

The meek are people humbly submissive to God; they recognise his hand and, instead of being angered by the prosperity of the wicked, remain patient and put their trust in God.

To have the “earth” as an inheritance becomes for them a prophetic symbol of the fullness of happiness. The verse “the meek shall possess the earth and enjoy great peace” (Ps 37:11) was surely alive in the heart of Saint Anne and, needless to say, in the heart of Mary, whom the Church greets: “O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary!”.

Precisely because Saint Anne was truly meek according to God's admonition, she merited to be the mother of the Immaculate, the “New Earth” from which Jesus was born, divine meekness made flesh.

The meekness of Jesus and of all who wish to be authentic followers of the divine Master is splendidly expressed by Saint John the Baptist when he presents Jesus to the crowds: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

The symbol of the Lamb is deeply evocative and meaningful: it speaks at once of meekness and of total readiness.

Jesus remains silent even as he is led to death; the meekness expressed in the figure of the Lamb sums up the whole Gospel, Jesus' character and his passion and death.

⟦p. 92⟧

The same symbol recurs in Saint John the Evangelist to express the resurrection and glorification of Jesus, the light that illumines Paradise: “The heavenly city has no need of the light of the sun or of the moon, for the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb” (Rev 21:23).

What reflections of Jesus, meek and humble of heart, the virtue of meekness contains, a characteristic of the charism of Mother Rosa and her disciples; what irresistible attraction it exercises on souls in the apostolate; and what fullness of self-mastery its constant practice implies! Meekness is a strong virtue that presupposes continual self-control in order to keep evenness and balance in one's words, unruffled consistency in dealing with others and serenity of conduct, despite adverse circumstances and the temperaments of the people we have to deal with each day. How much humanity and what spiritual labour this great virtue demands!

2.1. Experience of the freely given love of the God of the Covenant

Prayer is truly the cry of the poor in the deepest sense of the word. It is the cry of the creature that feels its nothingness before the All that is God.

Even before it is an experience of God, it is the experience of one's own creaturely limitation, which has received everything, continually receives everything and has nothing of itself. The poor can say only one thing to God: thank you!

⟦p. 93⟧

Jesus Christ willed to remain tangibly on earth as Eucharist, that is, as thanksgiving made person: a perennial and infinite thank-you to make reparation for our ingratitude and infidelity.

Before the infinite Eucharistic thanksgiving to God the Father, every prayer of ours must be permeated with boundless gratitude. Gratitude is the essential poverty, full of love, that says thank you to God, aware that, however much it receives, it always feels poor and in need of an ever greater abundance of graces and spiritual gifts. This is our experience of God's free and generous love. If we think in particular of the supernatural gifts, all unified and personified in Jesus – the Father's gift to humanity in the old Covenant as the promised Messiah and Saviour, and in the new Covenant as Emmanuel, the eternal Word made Man – then the gift of ourselves and of our prayer through Christ, with Christ, in Christ and by him to the Father becomes great, not without the active presence of the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son.

Saint Paul's thought therefore comes spontaneously to mind: “Being rich in infinite goods, he became poor with us and for us, to enrich us with the very riches of God.” Prayer is thus always a gift of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. On our part there then springs up spontaneously a thank-you that gives glory to and magnifies the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

⟦p. 94⟧

Saint Augustine says: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, prays for us. He prays for us as a holy priest and high priest, innocent, unstained, infinitely removed from sinners and higher than the heavens; he prays in us, he is prayed to by us” (Commentary on the Letter to the Hebrews, 7:26). Saint Fulgentius, Bishop, adds: “Jesus is for us God and temple of God, priest and sacrifice” (cf. Office of Readings, Friday of the Fifth Week of Lent).

Our prayer therefore forms one thing with Jesus' prayer. He is our priest, our perennial sacrifice, because the sacrifice of his passion and death accompanies every prayer of ours and gives it value. “Through our Lord Jesus Christ”, the Church sings. Through Jesus, with Jesus and in Jesus our prayer reaches the Father under the action of the Holy Spirit.

Jesus, as we said, is also the temple of our prayer. Why, then, in the old Covenant did God forbid and rebuke David, who wanted to build him the temple? The immediate answer is in Scripture itself: God had reserved this mission not for David but for his son, King Solomon (cf. 1 Kgs 5:17-19 and 2 Kgs 8:19).

⟦p. 95⟧

Widening our gaze to a vaster horizon, that of faith, we discover that things take on a grander and more fascinating meaning. Jesus himself says that he is a “Temple”: “Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). Jesus is our temple. From the moment of the incarnation he became the temple in which we must raise our prayer to the Father. The Church is our teacher, concluding every prayer “through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever”. What a temple! We are invited to remain in this temple continually.

God, however, was not content to give us so most holy a temple. He willed to adorn it with the most marvellous vestibule the hand of the supreme divine artist could design, or engrave in the soul and Immaculate Heart of Mary, and build, to the point of creating that divine masterpiece which is the mother of the Redeemer and of all humanity: “Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn seven pillars” (Prov 9:1).

With the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit he carved in Mary's soul the most splendid vestibule possible to the wise and mighty art of God, creator and restorer of fallen nature. When we wish to enter the temple that is Jesus Christ, the entrance is sure. But if Mary Most Holy is the vestibule that leads directly into the temple that is Jesus Christ, Saint Anne, the mother of the Immaculate, is the solemn prior architecture, also wrought by the Holy Spirit, that leads in a manner worthy of God to the vestibule and the temple. This follows logically.

⟦p. 96⟧

When we truly love the Lord, when we consider that he is more intimate to us than we are to ourselves, we end up making our whole life a dialogue of intimacy: of filial abandonment to the Father, in full adherence to the divine will, with total self-offering in every daily circumstance, in uninterrupted union with Jesus in the Eucharist; of docility to the Holy Spirit; of total surrender to the Most Holy Trinity; of tenderness towards Mary Most Holy, our most sweet mother; and of love and filial trust towards Saint Anne, the angels and the saints, just as Mother Rosa did.

The unsurpassable model of prayer for us remains the one taught by Jesus himself: “Our Father, who art in heaven”, which contains the truth of our sonship before God the creator, redeemer and sanctifier, and for that very reason also opens us to the experience of universal brotherhood with all the members of the human community, who, thanks to the mystery of the incarnation, become one family in Christ, in communion and in the sharing of the material and spiritual goods generously bestowed on all by God's infinite goodness.

All the members of the human family are either Christians or are called to know and love Jesus Christ. With him, in him and through him we can call our God “Father”.

Hence the urgency of missionary and evangelising activity, so that the “virtual” call may become actual and explicit through knowledge of the Gospel. While he was teaching the “Our Father”, Jesus was surrounded by his disciples. Today too he continues to be present among those who pray with faith. The scene of Jesus praying to the Father with his disciples has therefore become the paradigm of Christian prayer. When the Christian, consecrated persons, the whole Church and within it all the members of the Family of the holy Mother set themselves to pray, Jesus prays with them and they pray with the divine Master.

⟦p. 97⟧

But Christian prayer does not consist only in what Jesus teaches, the Our Father. The prayer of Christian prayers is the sacrifice of the Mass, which is at once adoration, praise, thanksgiving, reparation, petition and expiation. The deepest adoration coincides with the very sacrifice of the altar: the priest is the same, Jesus; the victim is the same, Jesus! Our most lovable redeemer, who is again Jesus, continues to be the Master of our prayer, not by words but by deeds, through his eternal, universal sacrifice, of infinite impetratory value, the source of every grace.

Our prayer therefore acquires value to the extent that it shares in the prayer-sacrifice of the Lord.

Since the sacrifice of the altar, the unbloody continuation of the sacrifice of the cross, is the model of our prayer, only by praying with Jesus do we become sharers in the redemption of the world, after the example of Mary Most Holy, who, by sharing in the prayer and in the mystery of her Son's redemption, became the Mediatrix and Mother of all people.

2.2. A loving, trusting, constant dialogue

Infused prayer, such as Mother Rosa experienced, is certainly a great gift of God. Before receiving such gifts from God, however, a simultaneous exercise of many virtues is needed, as we read in Mother Rosa's experience.

⟦p. 98⟧

It is not possible to pray well without full self-mastery over one's feelings, imagination and the worries caused by apostolic and educational work itself.

Prayer goes well, on the other hand, as dialogue with God deserves, when the person has overcome everything worldly and has won freedom of spirit through the spiritual combat that accompanies the ascetical phase of the interior life, even though in a sense the ascetical and combative phase of the spiritual life never ends.

Ascetical life and mystical life, as we have said, are the two components of the spiritual life.

In people far advanced in perfection the mystical aspect prevails; in others still on the way, or at any rate less advanced, the ascetical aspect often prevails. Saint Augustine, in his letter to Proba, says: “When we pray we should not lose ourselves in many considerations, trying to know what we ought to ask and fearing we shall not manage to pray. Why do we not rather say with the psalmist: ‘One thing I have asked of the Lord, this alone I seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life’…?” (Ps 26:4).

To dwell in the house of the Lord means nothing other than keeping ourselves continually in the presence of God, opening ourselves trustingly to him with a filial, attentive, loving and humble heart like Mary's, and being docile to his Word and its demands, until we experience perfect union with him.

⟦p. 99⟧

2.3. At the sources of prayer

The source of prayer is Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word, his Word and his example (see below, pp. 92-97).

The teacher of prayer is the Church with her liturgy, which leads us through and has us meditate on each of the mysteries of Jesus' life. The Church also helps us to pray with the liturgical prayers of the Mass.

Prayer is the weapon that makes the Kingdom of God advance in us and in the Church herself, as Mother Rosa testifies:

“My Love, make use for once of this wretched instrument to revive faith and the conversion of sinners” (M. 1,1, p. 60).

It is a gift of God because, by virtue of our sharing in the divine life, which is grace, it makes us sharers in the value and efficacy of Jesus' own prayer.

That is why the human person, when praying, performs the greatest work possible to a creature. Vital union with Jesus – “I am the vine, you are the branches” – is therefore of universal beneficial efficacy. Our prayer, sharing in Christ's sacrifice and prayer, takes on the dimensions of his very prayer.

⟦p. 100⟧

That is why even a simple ejaculatory prayer, said with faith and hope, is something immensely great, so that it is never right to say, “my prayer is worth little”. It would be worth little if it lacked the foundation of faith and were cut off from the prayer of Jesus Christ; but when the soul is in grace, its prayer cannot possibly be a small thing.

2.4. The battle of prayer

Jesus awaits our participation for the completion of his redeeming work. What Saint Paul says of himself holds for everyone and always: “in my flesh I complete what is lacking in Christ's afflictions” (Col 1:24).

It is the part each of us, individually and as a community, can add to the Saviour's redeeming work. In this sense we can say, “already and not yet!”.

Since prayer is a gift of such immense value, it is understandable that the devil does everything to prevent or spoil our prayer, either by disturbing our inner dispositions or by plotting “snares” of every kind against our recollection and silence. Hence the need for vigilance and careful preparation of the heart when we set ourselves to pray.

If there is good will on our part, the Holy Spirit will not fail to assist us by driving away the snares of the evil one, who is the enemy of prayer as he is the enemy of people, especially those seriously committed to the most important work of man on earth: growth in love and union with God, that is, on the way of holiness.

⟦p. 101⟧

2.5. The experience of being brothers and sisters in Christ Jesus

When we keep in mind our belonging to the Church and are firmly persuaded that we form one body and one Church with all Christians, prayer becomes universally choral. And if we are firmly convinced that the pilgrim Church and the heavenly Church are also one, then the angels and saints of Paradise surely echo our prayer.

A solid foundation is formed by the spiritual heritage of the Family of the mother of the Immaculate. “Following the example of Mother Rosa, the Daughters of Saint Anne [and all the members of her spiritual Family], ‘aiming solely and above all at God’, strive to join contemplation with apostolic service and, docile to the Holy Spirit, seek in the intimacy of prayer the encounter with the Father, so as to live with him, in imitation of Christ, a relationship of tender and intense filial love. Faithful, therefore, to Jesus' exhortation to pray without ceasing, and inspired by the poor and humble of the Lord who ‘with groans and sighs, tears and prayers’ (Rule of 1869, 1, 3°) prepared the coming of the Messiah, the Sisters [and Brothers] walk humbly with God (cf. Mic 6:8), seeking his face in the secret of their hearts and in the fraternal exchange of a communion of prayer centred on the Eucharist. In this way, persevering in prayer with Mary, the mother of Jesus, and proclaiming the death and resurrection of the Lord, they prepare with the whole Church for his full manifestation: ‘Come, Lord Jesus!’.

⟦p. 102⟧

Wholly devoted to the salvation of the world, a divine work that transcends all human strength and all human wisdom, the Sisters [and Brothers] commit themselves to discovering day by day, in the intimacy of personal and community dialogue with God, his saving will, and to opening themselves to the action of the Spirit so as to become docile instruments of the Father's mercy” (Constitutions, arts. 48-49).

The Constitutions and statutes thus sum up and express the foundress's thought: “I have no other treasure than prayer.”

In the old Covenant Christ himself is the source of prayer; the chosen people looked to him, announced by the Prophets as the future Messiah, and in Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate, that people will find the synthesis, strengthened by her eminent holiness, the concentrated conclusion of all the prayers of the patriarchs, the prophets and the saints of Israel: “Come and delay no longer!” More than words, theirs was an attitude of continual prayer, the sigh of the heart that in Saint Anne reached the summit of efficacy and intercession.

And she was heard, more than anyone before her, precisely in being chosen as mother of the Mother of the promised Redeemer, of her who by her immaculate and most powerful prayer would obtain the grace of graces: the descent of the Redeemer to earth, through her own immaculate person, filled to the highest degree with every grace and every choicest virtue.

⟦p. 103⟧

2.6. Mary, woman of listening and prayer

“Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you. Behold, you will conceive a son, give birth to him and call him Jesus. He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign for ever over the house of Jacob, and his kingdom will have no end” (Luke 1:28-33).

Mary Most Holy's prayer brought the hope of the long waiting to its most joyful conclusion. From that moment there will take place the first coming of the One who sums up in himself all creation and all redemption: birth, life, passion, death and resurrection, and the new era of hope will begin: in the return of Jesus in glory.

Mary Most Holy is the guarantor of our hope; that is why we call on her: “After this exile show us Jesus”, O Mary, first in the clear light of faith, then in the dazzling and beatifying light of glory. This is the longing of our souls, especially when prayer becomes our breath every day and every moment.

This prayer guides us to ever more intimate union with God and to spending our life in charity towards God and neighbour, that is, walking in holiness.

The prayer of the new Covenant does not exclude but includes the prayer of Saint Anne, in which the whole prayer of the old Covenant meets, is perfected and is consummated.

⟦p. 104⟧

Jesus is our programme, our goal and the meaning of our apostolate in all its forms, in the footsteps and after the model of Mary Most Holy, our “ideal” as Daughters [and Sons] of Saint Anne.

In this perspective, where the spirituality of the two Covenants comes alive again, the goal of the vocation of the daughters of Saint Anne and of the other members of the Family of the mother of the Immaculate takes on its full meaning: to walk towards holiness by identifying with Christ in the mystery of his poverty, so as to cooperate in the Church in his saving work through a service of motherly and fatherly dedication to their brothers and sisters, under the guidance of Saint Anne, mother of Mary Immaculate. Rooted, through the holy mother of Mary Immaculate, in the spirituality of the “Poor of Yahweh”, who lived awaiting the Messiah and seeking his face, they too live for Jesus Christ, who became “poor” to enrich us with his graces and with every supernatural good (cf. Const., art. 6).

This broad sense of poverty enables us to understand that the true wealth is Jesus, with whom consecrated souls, and all who truly wish to become holy, feel the urgency of identifying themselves by making their own his poverty, his humility, his thirst for redemptive suffering, imitating Mary, who becomes for all the ideal lived to the highest degree possible for a mere creature.

⟦p. 105⟧

The daughters [and sons] of Saint Anne and the other members of the Family follow Christ, the poor one par excellence, and contemplate Mary, who not only stands out among the humble and poor of the Lord but surpasses them beyond comparison, so as to draw God's gaze: “He has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid.” Precisely because of this supreme poverty she was filled with the fullness of grace on earth, and of glory in heaven and throughout the centuries of human history: “All generations will call me blessed.”

In the Magnificat Mary reveals the praying soul that sums up in itself, in mature form, the praise, blessing, adoration, supplication, offering, expectation and gratitude of her forebears, that is, of all who glorified God with their lives.

She draws reasons for contemplation and rejoicing from her own personal experience of God, in whom she perceives herself as a link in the long chain of human history.

Formed in the contemplation of the events and wonders of God handed down by Scripture, shaped early in the sense of personal relationship with him, as an authentic “poor one”, her prayer becomes absolute openness and docility when the mysterious event of the Incarnation involves her personally. Prayer trains her to grasp every passage of God in her own history and in that of humanity; that is why she proclaims him: my Saviour, Almighty and Holy.

⟦p. 106⟧

The contemplation of God detaches her from herself to such a degree that she sees herself in him as a “handmaid” who, by her humility and littleness, has drawn the divine blessing upon humanity. As a chosen member of the “Remnant of Israel”, Mary nourishes her prayer with the Word of God, and welcomes into her soul the message of the psalms, turning it into a living fabric that lights her action and opens her to the universal embrace of her Saviour's saving work.

Union with God, the specific vocation of her people, is achieved in her to such a degree that she becomes, by God's free grace, the Mother of the eternal Word: the Messiah awaited by Israel, the Redeemer who, associating her with his redeeming plan, makes her Mother of Humanity.

Contemplating Mary, the members of the Family of the holy Mother live their commitment in the Church in prayer and poverty of heart, which for them is a way of being, living and existing that marks their presence in the world and shapes their family and apostolic way of life.

Contemplation, prayer, “poverty of heart, which Mother Rosa embodied in her own life, driven by her ardent desire to identify with Christ emptied even to death on a cross, with him whom she used to call ‘my Good’ and whose very way she longed to walk, her gaze turned towards Mary as the perfect model of what she experienced as her most intimate vocation: ‘Useless slave of my Jesus, my beloved Paradise’” (Const., art. 6).

The emphasis on Mary's presence has great and exceptional significance for the Daughters of Saint Anne and Mother Rosa's other followers, and reveals their spirit. In harmony with their very name, it designates them as sisters and brothers of Mary Most Holy, formed in the same school and continuers of her mission.

Covenant and Hope are two themes that contain the whole spiritual life of the Old and New Testaments. There is, however, an easily identifiable difference between them.

In the OT the Covenant was founded on a pact and a promise between God and his people.

A pact clearly presupposes the presence and acquaintance of the persons who agree on the pact itself and, naturally, on its content.

The OT Covenant is therefore founded on God's promise of the Mediator between himself and mankind, able to reconcile humanity after the grave rupture of disobedience and of the offence against him who had deigned to create man free and admit him to his friendship. Making man a member of the family, God treats him as the members of a human family treat one another. Such a pact implied the supreme God's extreme condescension towards the poor creaturely reality of man, even though made in his image and likeness.

⟦p. 110⟧

By delaying for centuries the fulfilment of the promise contained in the pact, God almost makes us touch the abyss of misery into which sin had cast man, turning the earthly paradise into a valley of tears (Gen 3:14-19), beginning with the murder of Abel by his brother Cain (cf. Gen 4:8), a crime that then spread into the fratricidal wars of Israel's history, aggravated by an unbroken series of sufferings, defeats, enslavements and violence. It is precisely this train of evils that rekindles hope in the Saviour.

Israel's hope thus becomes a deep desire full of anguish, felt all the more keenly the surer was faith in the fulfilment of the promises by him who does not and cannot deceive and who, above all, never fails to show his goodness and mercy in deeds.

Yet the old Covenant often fell into crisis, not on God's part but on that of his people. It is enough to recall what happened on the way from Egypt to the promised land: the repeated complaints against Moses were in fact complaints against God, who had chosen Moses as a strong and faithful leader and guide. And how many times Moses had to appease God's anger at the infidelity of his people, who went so far as to replace him with an idol, the golden calf, made by Aaron and celebrated as their true God. And this after so many proofs of wondrous and fatherly assistance.

⟦p. 111⟧

Infidelity to the Covenant was in any case repeated many times in the history of the chosen people. God then sent great Prophets to remind the people of the divine promises, prophets who were almost always ill-treated and even put to death.

All this shows the fragility of a Covenant that rests on men on the one hand and on the word of God on the other. And to the extent that the Covenant falls into crisis, hope falls into crisis. God, however, never fails his word. And when the people abandon him, he comes to meet them with the wonders of his mercy.

In this way we understand how the whole history of Israel is the living history of God's mercy towards his people, for his mercy is infinite, as the Psalms say. This mercy renews hope again and again, concentrated and rekindled in the saints and above all in the splendid holiness of the mother of the Immaculate and of Mary, her daughter.

God willed to give hope a foundation of absolute firmness in the new Covenant through an indissoluble union between himself and man in the mystery of the incarnation, a Covenant above every possible crisis, indeed a Covenant that would never again fall into crisis because it is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, a union of absolute security between God and humanity, he remaining for ever truly God and truly man.

⟦p. 112⟧

It is a matter of accepting in faith this wonderful encounter of the Word with humanity. Here lies the basis of the hope that will unite in Jesus Christ the fullness of human nature and the fullness of the divine nature. On this basis hope can no longer suffer crises or infidelities, for these are overcome in Christ, who can promptly and divinely heal the infidelities of individuals and of his people, the mystical body of the Church.

Through the Church the people of God are united to Christ, the incarnate Word, as his Bride, as his mystical body. Not even the powers of hell can crack this divine covenant, which thus acquires a stability as strong as God's omnipotence. Here is the new and divinely stable foundation of hope in the New Testament.

Yet the freedom of the individual is not taken away. The individual may refuse to accept it, but can no longer break it, though he may deny it and be lost.

To bring man back within the Covenant, Jesus instituted the sacrament of Mercy, for whoever repents and is fully readmitted to intimacy with God, and the sacrament of the Eucharist, which identifies and transforms him to such a degree as to make him one with himself, almost divinising him.

⟦p. 113⟧

The NT Covenant is therefore made unbreakable by the indissoluble union of the divine nature with the human nature assumed in the divine Person of the incarnate Word. Personally united to God, man takes on a sublime dignity: the dignity of Christ himself. The NT Covenant is, as already said, as indissoluble as the human nature is inseparable from the divine in the person of Christ. To the extent that we share in Christ's divine nature through the Sacraments, we enter this covenant. All the Sacraments graft us into God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, through Jesus Christ, from baptism to the Eucharist, which is at once sacrifice and sacrament: “I am the living bread come down from Heaven. Whoever eats this bread lives in me and I in him, and will have eternal life.” Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas say that the Eucharistic bread is not like the bread on our tables, which is changed into us and becomes our flesh, blood and bones. On the contrary, the Eucharistic bread has the power to transform us and identify us with Christ, to make us one with him in the measure of our faith.

Mother Rosa perceived its effects in her mystical experience, which is why she exclaimed: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.”

Jesus prayed and prays thus: “Father, I pray that they may be one: I in them and you in me, that they may be brought to perfection in unity” (John 17:22-23).

The new Covenant therefore involves us to the point of being, with Jesus and in Jesus, one with the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; it involves us not only as members of the mystical body and of the people of God which is the Church, but also personally. The NT Covenant is not only a covenant with a people but God's covenant with each individual person, because God knows us personally and each person is everything to God, as if he or she were the only reality he had created. Not for nothing did he will to reach us with the motherly tenderness of a Mother.

Each of us before God is therefore an only son, an only daughter, and so infinitely beloved. In Christ Jesus we all share in his uniqueness, in God the Father's infinite benevolence towards his Only-begotten.

⟦p. 114⟧

In Jesus we are loved by the Father as the Father loves the Son, who loved us even to death on the cross.

What wonder the reality of the new Covenant contains, and to what wealth of perfection Jesus brought it! The greatness, security and indissolubility of the new make us appreciate the old better. The wonderful bond of the redeeming Covenant becomes a magnificent reason and foundation for hope.

In this perspective, Christian life and holiness rest on pivots so firm that they cannot fail to become a witness for those who accept and live them fully, proclaiming them by life, example, word and action that becomes charity towards God and towards their brothers and sisters.

It is not possible to identify with Jesus through prayer and the sacraments, above all the Eucharist, without becoming one with him. And since Jesus is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, Mother Rosa's spiritual Family fulfils Jesus' thought and example by letting itself be guided by the Spirit along the path that leads it to full adherence to the Father's will and to perfect communion with him.

1.1. Called to live communion in their respective states of life

⟦p. 115⟧

The daughters of Saint Anne and the other members of the Family of the holy mother of Mary Immaculate, called to express the Covenant, nourish fraternal communion in hope. Heirs of the community spirit of the “remnant of Israel”, in which Anne, Joachim and Mary stand out, gathered in the name of the Lord, faithful to the unity Jesus willed, striving for fraternal love, the emblem of the Family, they live like Mary a stance of openness to God in all circumstances and situations, their hearts full of attention to their brothers and sisters in Jesus Christ.

Throughout the history of the Covenant-Hope, love holds a privileged place: “I love the Lord, for he hears the voice of my prayer” (Ps 116:1). “As a child whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you… when you see it, your heart shall rejoice” (Isa 66:13-14). God's love for his people was fulfilled in the coming of the Messiah in a way beyond all human expectation.

The first to welcome him is Mary, the Daughter of Saint Anne.

By fulfilling his promises in her, the luminous dawn of the world's new era, and through her in her family, which contains all the hope of the old Covenant, the Lord gives a response of love to the faithful love of her holy parents Joachim and Anne. Love rooted in the Covenant not only makes them God's own possession but unites them with each other, opening them to the needs of their neighbour: “Give justice to the weak and the orphan, uphold the right of the afflicted and the poor, rescue the wretched and the needy from the hand of the wicked, rescue them!” (Ps 82:3-4).

⟦p. 116⟧

It is precisely interpersonal relationships that reveal the God of the Covenant; this happens when the whole set of virtues outlined in the Rule of 1869 and emphasised in the Constitutions renewed after Vatican II is put into practice.

Bearing in mind that the perfect practice of one virtue includes the practice of all the others, when the soul is wholly open to awaiting Jesus, the sublime theological virtues – faith, hope and charity – flower simultaneously.

The whole range of Christian virtues cannot go beyond what Saint Paul says of charity, which will always be the charism of charisms, giving warmth to all the other virtues, becoming their mother and handmaid, summing up in itself every other virtue and transfiguring it into love of God and neighbour. “And I will show you a still more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels but have not charity, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have the gift of prophecy and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and have faith so as to move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. If I give away all I have and deliver my body to be burned, but have not charity, I gain nothing” (1 Cor 12:31–13:3).

⟦p. 117⟧

Charity therefore sums up the practice of all the virtues: “it is patient and kind; charity is not envious, it does not boast, it is not puffed up, it is not disrespectful, it does not seek its own interest, it is not irritable, it keeps no record of wrongs received, it does not rejoice in injustice but rejoices in the truth. It covers all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor 13:4-7).

Are not the virtues Mother Rosa held so dear – simplicity, humility, meekness, prudence – so many forms of charity? These virtues are no less the companions of hope. One cannot have a great love for God and neighbour without the sure horizon of hope. Faith, hope and charity are inseparable components of Christian perfection; they form its substance. This is especially true when these virtues are lived in the generous gratuitousness and readiness proper to a “poor and merciful” heart, intent only on growing in mutual communion. Therefore, to live the family spirit in the various states of life, according to the particular vocation of Rosa Gattorno's disciples, means: giving oneself generously to one another, as God does (cf. 2 Cor 9:5-14); living mutual understanding, tolerance and respect for the truth present in everyone (cf. Rom 14); placing the Father at the centre of mutual relationships, welcoming his Word and letting oneself be transformed by it; sacrificing oneself after the example of Christ Jesus, intent on reaching the goal he pointed out: “if we love one another… God's love is perfected in us” (1 John 4:12).

1.2. Co-responsibility in fraternal life

⟦p. 118⟧

The Church is essentially a mystery of communion, “a people gathered in the unity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit” (cf. LG 4).

Fraternal life mirrors the depth and richness of this mystery, taking shape as a human space inhabited by the Trinity, which thus extends into history the gifts of communion proper to the three divine persons.

All this requires a path of personal and community growth: learning to overcome conflicts, growing in the capacity to forgive, in the exercise of discernment in the light of the Holy Spirit, knowing how to create unity in diversity, fostering and taking part in dialogue, after the unattainable model of Mary Most Holy.

All the members of Mother Rosa's charismatic Family are called to bear one another's burdens with love, loving the cross as she did, remaining serene in trials and joyful in hope, never forgetting that a charism lived to the full translates the Gospel, in particular the Gospel of the beatitudes, proclaimed by Jesus in his programmatic discourse, in which he makes us understand that every virtue and every suffering and contradiction borne for love of God brings into the soul a beginning of Paradise, in constant remembrance of the suffering Jesus and of Mary Immaculate and Sorrowful, mother of Grace and Mercy, mother of Hope.

To live a way of life that witnesses to fraternity and proclaims hope, however, requires a deep life of prayer and of freely given self-gift.

⟦p. 119⟧

2.1. The daughters of Saint Anne

and the other members of the Family

of the holy Mother of Mary Immaculate,

faithful to the covenant,

strengthen in hope

their communion with God

The ideal of Mother Rosa's charism, handed on and faithfully lived by the daughters of Saint Anne, and now also by the other members of the Family of the holy mother of Mary Immaculate, calls for an uncommon spirit of offering and prayer, the primary sources of holiness and apostolic effectiveness, in the following of Mary Most Holy, who, as already recalled, stands out among the poor and humble of all times.

It is a persevering prayer, made in faith and hope, in a continual crescendo of intimate relationship with God, ever more habitual and continuous. The simple but profound saying of the Mother foundress, “I have no other treasure than prayer”, truly contains the great and most precious treasure for personal sanctification and for the apostolate.

⟦p. 120⟧

When prayer becomes the only treasure, guarded and increased day after day, the daughters and sons of the mother of the Immaculate, and all who have received from God the privilege of living the charism of this distinguished religious Family, can walk with full certainty towards the encounter with Christ, so as to give him with sure effectiveness to their brothers and sisters in the labours of their apostolate.

Prayer, Mother Rosa's “only treasure”, lays the foundations of apostolic activity as the spontaneous and consequent projection of the interior life.

Otherwise the person remains empty and apostolic action sterile and fruitless. With what strong supernatural realism the Constitutions state: “Wholly devoted to the salvation of the world, a divine work that transcends all human strength and all human wisdom, the Sisters [and Brothers] commit themselves to discovering day by day, in the intimacy of personal and community dialogue with God, his saving will, and to opening themselves to the action of the Spirit so as to become docile instruments of the Father's mercy.”

“Aware of Mother Rosa's priceless spiritual heritage, her daughters and those who follow her and live her message will cultivate prayer, applying themselves every day to meditation on Sacred Scripture [according to the Constitutions and statutes of each form of life in which the same charism is lived].

Interiorising the Word is not possible without the inner silence that allows us to hear God, who manifests himself as “the whisper of a gentle breeze”, speaks to the heart and asks his creatures: “Be silent and listen.”

⟦p. 121⟧

Very aptly and acutely the Constitutions further state: “To create the conditions most favourable to prayer, it is essential that each one practise an asceticism that develops and strengthens the spiritual integration of his or her tendencies and the practice of the virtues proper to the Institute, so as to make the community [and the spiritual family] the place where the face of the Lord is sought together” (Const., no. 49, a, b, c; own Statutes). Every word of these paragraphs is of supreme importance for the consecrated person and for all who intend to live and work in Mother Rosa's charism. Many things are said explicitly in these lines, but still more truths are implicit, easily read between the lines.

From the whole context, however, it is evident that the “silence” to be cultivated is not only the outward silence of words but above all inward silence: that of the heart which knows how to quiet the reactions of nature and the noise of the outside world. What is needed, however, is the full liberation of soul and heart, so that the Spirit may make felt his presence and his continual inspirations, delicate as the whisper of a gentle breeze. The Holy Spirit took possession of the soul at baptism and then, in ever greater abundance, through the other sacraments, and most particularly at the solemn moment of religious profession or of the act of acceptance to live according to Mother Rosa's spirit and charism.

All who wish to follow her spirit and example truly intend to live to the full the grace of adoption as sons and daughters of God.

Saint Paul warns: “Only those who are led by the Holy Spirit, only these are truly children of God.”

⟦p. 122⟧

It is consoling that, especially since the Second Vatican Council, the Spirit is bringing to fulfilment all the expressions he had already shown mystically to the foundress Rosa Gattorno in the last century. Many, drawn by her, are in fact learning to let themselves be guided by the Holy Spirit and put first in their Christian life the continual search for the face of God.

To be guided by the Spirit, to seek the face of God, to adhere to his will turns life into a continual, unceasing “conversion”. In its deep etymological sense this word means “turning towards” God continually, with an ever more intense and victorious effort to fight against the assaults of the deafening noise of the world, which besieges us, especially today, more forcefully than ever, in proportion to the multiplication of the ever more numerous and insidious means of social communication. The more we free our hearts from outward din, the more the Holy Spirit can communicate himself and guide the soul to holiness and apostolic zeal.

The Constitutions and Statutes list the means of cultivating silence and inner peace. Prayer is always the greatest work we can do, because it involves the contact of our spirit with God in Christ Jesus, the Mediator by essence and by nature, and with Mary Most Holy, the universal mediatrix with the Son, the one Mediator between God and humanity.

The mystery of Christ, priest and victim of the new and eternal Covenant, therefore contains and illuminates the greatness and power of Christian prayer.

⟦p. 123⟧

2.2. In the celebration of the Eucharist

Jesus, the divine victim, is present in the Eucharistic celebration, revealing himself through the Sacrament as an eternal presence that walks with humanity.

The Mass is exactly the same, identical sacrifice that Jesus offered in blood on Calvary amid unspeakable pain and the shedding of all his Blood. Our prayer is grafted into the very prayer of Christ, truly man but also, by nature, God and a divine Person.

The second Person of the Most Holy Trinity, in Jesus Christ as divine person, extends his active presence to all times and all places, embracing and surpassing them all. Before God all times and all persons existing in time form a single present: the present of eternity.

⟦p. 124⟧

The sacrifice of the cross, which took place in time, always remains the identical sacrifice inscribed in the light of divine eternity. By instituting the Eucharist Jesus made his sacrifice perpetually present. During the celebration of the sacrifice of the Mass we are all simultaneously and personally present at the foot of the cross with Mary Most Holy and Saint John. When we pray, Jesus prays with us and we with him. Our prayer then takes on the meaning, value and efficacy of Jesus' prayer, the essential prayer of infinite value, to which ours is joined as sacrifice and therefore as adoration, saying to God: “You are everything, you are my Creator and Redeemer; I come from nothing and from your infinite love. As far as I am concerned, then, I am nothing, and I express this condition of mine before you by emptying myself with Jesus on the cross.”

Uniting myself with Jesus in “You are everything and I am nothing”: this is the prayer of adoration. It is precisely this self-emptying, this sincere profession of one's own nothingness, that places one within the All that is Jesus.

Living in Jesus, with Jesus and for Jesus, we share in salvation, which presupposes atonement for sin. Thanks to the atonement of the merciful Jesus, to the full and total reparation he made, thanks to the infinite value of the essential praise offered to the Father by Jesus on the cross, our prayer at holy Mass becomes one with the praise Jesus gives to the Father. With Jesus, in Jesus, through Jesus we too raise an infinite praise to the Father. But the sacrifice of the altar is, in a still more essential way, “the Eucharist”, that is, the radical “thank you” to God. Not for nothing did Jesus will to remain always with us under the veils of bread and wine as a perennial, infinite prayer of thanksgiving.

The only response, the only thing the creature can then offer to the Creator from whom it has received everything, is to enter into that “radical thank you”. Nothingness (which is what the creature is) can give nothing else.

⟦p. 125⟧

That is why Jesus willed to remain with us as Eucharist, that is, as thanksgiving made Person, the thanksgiving of eternal and infinite love. In this above all Jesus made himself our teacher, not in words but in deeds, through the miracle of miracles that is the Eucharist. He was not even content to become our teacher of prayer. By becoming a perennial sacrifice he willed to make of us so many living “thank-yous”, becoming bread, a bread that transforms, divinises and conforms to Christ.

The more we are transformed by the Eucharist, the more we too become living Eucharists, souls whose whole life is and must be an unceasing thank-you. We give thanks with the “thank you” of words, with the thanks of mind and heart, with the thanks of work, of sacrifice, of total dedication to the good of others, eager to pour our Eucharistic spirit into the people we meet, so as to transform them too into so many living Eucharists.

The Eucharist is the source of all prayer; it is the bread that unites our prayer with that of the angels, the foretaste of Paradise, of eternal life, the foretaste of the adoration, praise and eternal, infinite thanksgiving that is the whole of Paradise. The Eucharist is the life of our life, the sacrament of Sacraments, the mystery of mysteries, which day by day works in us death to the world and its fleeting flatteries and prepares our whole personal reality for the encounter and eternal union with the risen Christ.

2.3. In the celebration of the Sacraments, channels of grace

⟦p. 126⟧

Besides the ineffable encounter in the sacrament of the Eucharist (sacrifice and communion), through the sacrament of penance Jesus refines and deepens the faith given us in baptism, by which God “delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Col 1:13).

By virtue of this sacrament we adhere to Christ and live in him; we have been given grace, that is, the divine life, which, in order to transform us into God, requires free and ever more responsible cooperation on our part.

With confirmation, which completes baptism, we become aware that spiritual growth is the work of the Holy Spirit, who with his gifts shapes in us the image of Christ Jesus.

The Father “saved us in his mercy through a washing of regeneration and renewal in the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ” (Titus 3:5-6).

With the sacrament of penance the “washing of regeneration” is renewed in us.

Returning from the confessional, Saint Catherine of Siena, doctor of the Church, would exclaim: “I have been to wash my soul in the Blood of Christ.”

This is truly what happens in every encounter with Christ in the sacrament of mercy.

⟦p. 127⟧

The daughters of Saint Anne and all the members of the Family of the mother of the Immaculate live in the sacrifice of Christ, who never ceases to intercede with the Father on our behalf: “Such was the high priest we needed: holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners and exalted above the heavens; he has no need, like the other priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, for he did this once for all when he offered himself” (Heb 7:26-27).

Closely united to Jesus' unceasing prayer for us and with us is the prayer of the mother of God, Mary Most Holy, who offers for us to the adorable Trinity the most sacred heart of Jesus, his perfect adoration, his unspeakable love, his eminent holiness, for God's greater glory, for the salvation of the world and the release of the souls in Purgatory, always imploring from Jesus forgiveness for the many offences committed against God, especially in our time. It is she who, while helping us to advance each day on the way of virtue and perfection, turns God's chastisements away from us.

God's gaze resting on her who is Immaculate and refuge of sinners always finds in her every pleasure and every delight.

Humanity, in the luminous transparency of Mary Most Holy, finds in her intercession and defence.

2.4. In the celebration of Mary, daughter of Saint Anne

From knowledge of the mystery of Christ follow love and devotion for his mother.

Those who in every generation, among the various peoples and nations of the earth, welcome with faith the mystery of Christ, the incarnate Word and redeemer of the world, not only turn with veneration and have recourse with trust to Mary as his Mother, but seek in her faith support for their own faith (cf. RM 27).

⟦p. 128⟧

If Mary, his Mother and ours, is present in our prayer with Jesus, our prayer reaches the Father more pleasing and more effective, for our personal salvation and for that of so many souls who today are so far from God.

In this spiritual horizon the daughters of Saint Anne and the other members of the Family of the holy mother of Mary Immaculate, awaiting the Lord who comes, attune their prayer to that of the Church, which from the beginning of her earthly journey has contemplated the Mother of God and constantly repeats with her the words of the Magnificat. They contemplate her with special devotion as daughter of Saint Anne and as her extension in the history of salvation. With the Church they love her and seek to become like her; they keep a bond that embraces the saving mystery she represents – past, present and future – and venerate her as the spiritual mother of humanity, mother of Grace and Mercy.

3.1. The daughters of Saint Anne

and the other members of the Family, awaiting the Lord who comes, build the kingdom in poverty of heart and motherly and fatherly self-giving

⟦p. 129⟧

Working in the Church according to a specific mission, they cooperate in Christ's saving work, carrying in their hearts a single passion: the Kingdom of God and the glory of the Father, after the foundress's example.

They therefore work for the growth of the holy faith, the conversion of sinners and the service of their brothers and sisters, made a sign and instrument of the Father's merciful love for all people. Inserted in the reality of the local Church, they are a leaven of communion within it, witnesses of hope and a presence that proclaims, and they build the kingdom in poverty of heart and motherly and fatherly self-giving.
