Just as Saint Anne awaited the fulfilment of the promises, the One sent by the Father, so they too, while hoping for the Lord's glorious manifestation, burning with zeal like Mother Rosa, strive to make him known to the whole world, certain that God has done, does and will continue to do great things in people through prayer and through our hard-working apostolic activity, even when the cross of Jesus, physical or spiritual, invites us to walk, at least in part, the way of Calvary.

It is the cross and the Crucified that Mother Rosa loved with such ardour and generous devotion, just as the Psalm says: “Lord, my rock and my fortress, my deliverer, my God, my crag where I take refuge, my shield and stronghold, my mighty salvation. The waves of death surrounded me, raging torrents overwhelmed me; deadly snares were already closing on me. In my distress I called on the Lord, in anguish I cried to my God; from his temple he heard my voice, my cry reached his ears” (Psalm 18:3.7).

⟦p. 130⟧

These words of the Psalm aptly foreshadow the great sufferings, mystical ones included, of the Mother foundress, who knew how to unite hope and love, joy and sorrow, “rejoicing like a champion running his course” (Psalm 19:6).

She knew how to walk the way of holiness and the apostolate in the footsteps of the suffering and crucified Christ, almost repeating with Jesus: “There is a baptism I must receive – the baptism of blood – and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12:50). And the words spoken on the eve of the passion: “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15).

3.2. In the Church, with a specific mission

Choosing Mary Immaculate as their model, they become a sign of hope for people today through preferential action for the poorest, knowing how to recognise and relieve new forms of poverty. They therefore work for integral liberation, in the sense of that freedom with which Christ has set us free (as Saint Paul says). Christ set us free so that we might remain free: “Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be burdened again with the yoke of slavery” (Gal 5:1).

⟦p. 131⟧

This is the great freedom that springs from Christ's redeeming death. An immensely deep freedom that ransoms man from slavery to Satan and sin, not in the narrow sense of mere “political” freedom to which Christ's freedom is sometimes reduced, but in the sense of integral freedom, a prophetic sign of hope for people today.

3.3. Credible witnesses, so that all people may open themselves to salvation

The daughters of Saint Anne and all who belong to the Family of the Mother of the Immaculate are called to be a prophetic sign of the Father's merciful love, of Christ Jesus' unconditional self-offering, of hope, the fruit of the Spirit.

By their very presence they seek to be credible witnesses for all people, so that they may open themselves to salvation and share in the integral freedom brought by Christ. They therefore comfort, help and make their own the anxieties and worries of those who suffer; they bring relief to the sick and the marginalised, awakening their hope in the Lord Jesus and his promises, and help them discover the precious essence of suffering in the light of his passion.

In the suffering and the marginalised they also recognise and serve the Crucified Christ, who regards as done to himself whatever is done to the weakest, the most forgotten and the poorest; and they accompany people's hopes with trust, directing them towards the way of the covenant that will be definitively fulfilled in the beatific vision, in the splendour of the Father's glory contemplated for ever.

⟦p. 132⟧

To achieve this they follow the action of the Spirit with watchful readiness and work hard to gather the whole human family around the Father, certain that only God and his Kingdom are absolute.

And so, with the whole Church, in prayer and with their hearts, they cry day and night: Come, Lord Jesus!

The goal the Lord points out to us as fullness of life in him implies movement, a striving towards communion with him, the object of our hope, and constant discernment so as to leave aside whatever might hinder the attainment of that end.

We find this essential condition of the “race” towards God in the inspired texts, in the teaching of the Church and in the example of the saints, not least in Mother Rosa.

The radical nature of her spiritual drive to advance swiftly towards the goal is fully confirmed by the pedagogy God shows throughout the Bible, but it appears even more clearly in certain texts:

⟦p. 136⟧

“whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have let all these things go and regard them as rubbish, in order to gain Christ and be found in him, not with a righteousness of my own based on the law, but with that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith; that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death, in the hope of attaining the resurrection from the dead. Not that I have already obtained the prize or am already perfect; I only strive to run so as to win it, because Jesus Christ has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have arrived; this alone I know: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I run towards the goal for the prize to which God calls us on high in Christ Jesus” (cf. Phil 3:7-14).

Here, then, is a sacred text inspired by God that clearly defines the vocation to holiness in general and in particular illuminates the spiritual path Mother Rosa left as a legacy to the Institute she founded.

This is the spirituality of the Covenant:

  • of the old Covenant, resting on the historical experience of God, on the Law;

  • of the new Covenant, rooted primarily in faith in Jesus Christ.

⟦p. 137⟧

It is precisely faith in him, in his divinity, that fills the soul with hope and supernatural optimism.

renewing power and sanctifying grace in the people of the new Covenant

1.1. Holiness, the loving plan of the faithful and merciful God

Through holiness “the people of God will grow in abundant fruit, as is splendidly shown in the history of the Church by the lives of so many saints” (cf. LG 40).

“In the various kinds of life and the various offices, one and the same holiness is cultivated by all who are moved by the Spirit of God and who, obedient to the voice of the Father and worshipping God the Father in spirit and in truth, follow the poor Christ, humble and bearing the cross, so as to deserve to share in his glory. Each one, according to his own gifts and functions, must advance without delay along the way of a living faith, which kindles hope and works through charity” (LG 41).

All Christians without exception must walk this way.

Here we have the substance of Christian holiness: “God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16).

⟦p. 138⟧

“God has poured out his love abundantly into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (cf. Rom 5:5); we must therefore consciously welcome the gift that is within us and that enables us to love him and our fellow human beings in him and for him.

The gift God has given us demands vigilance and attention to every Word that comes from him, which enlightens and helps us to do his will. It is through his Word, interpreted by the Church, that we understand the intrinsic value of the sacraments and the need to share in Christ's life through them.

The love God has poured into our hearts makes us devote ourselves constantly to prayer, urges us to self-denial and commits us to the active exercise of every virtue.

Charity, as the bond of perfection and the fulfilment of the law (cf. Col 3:14; Rom 13:10), governs all the means of sanctification, gives them form and brings them to completion. That is why the true disciple of Christ is marked by charity towards both God and neighbour, since Jesus Christ showed his charity by giving his life for us: no one has greater love than he who lays down his life for his brothers (cf. John 15:13).

Christians are called to bear witness before others, and especially before those who persecute them, to the love, the charity, the gift they have received, even at the risk of their lives. Martyrdom, if need be, makes them like the Master, who freely accepts death for the salvation of the world. And as Lumen Gentium 42 teaches, “All must be ready to confess Christ before men and to follow him along the way of the cross through the persecutions that the Church never lacks.”

⟦p. 139⟧

Other means the Lord offers to promote the holiness of the Church are the counsels he proposes to his disciples (cf. Matt 19:11; 1 Cor 7:7), so that more easily, with an undivided heart (cf. 1 Cor 7:32-34), they may consecrate themselves to God alone in virginity and celibacy. This perfect continence for the sake of the kingdom of heaven has always been held in singular honour by the Church as a sign and stimulus of charity and a special source of spiritual fruitfulness in the world.

1.2. Christ Jesus, the Holy One by essence, is the One who makes “all the saints”

⟦p. 140⟧

The Church recalls the apostle's admonition, who, urging the faithful to charity, exhorts them to have in themselves the same mind that was in Christ Jesus, who emptied himself, taking the nature of a servant, becoming obedient unto death (cf. Phil 2:7-8), and who for our sake, though he was rich, became poor (cf. 2 Cor 8:9). While the disciples must always show the imitation of and witness to this charity and humility of Christ, mother Church rejoices to find within her many men and women who follow more closely this self-emptying of the Saviour and show it more clearly by embracing poverty and renouncing their own will; for the love of God, in matters concerning perfection, they submit themselves to man beyond the strict measure of the precept, so as to conform themselves more fully to the obedient Christ. All the faithful, therefore, are invited and obliged to pursue holiness and the perfection of their own state. Let all strive, then, to direct their affections rightly, so that the use of the things of this world and attachment to riches, contrary to the spirit of evangelical poverty, may not prevent them from tending towards perfect charity, as the apostle warns: “Let those who use this world not settle down in it, for the form of this world is passing away” (cf. LG 42).

These texts, chosen from among the many inspired ones, form a brief and complete summary of spiritual doctrine and, more precisely, the best commentary on the programme: “Reaching out towards the fullness of communion with the God of the Covenant, the fulfilment of every hope”.

1.3. The Trinity, source and origin of all holiness

Holiness is the purpose of creation and redemption. “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev 11:44; 11:45; 19:2; 20:7; 20:26; 21:8), God had already said to the chosen people of the old Covenant, and one may say that all God's interventions, directly or indirectly through the Prophets, are a call to holiness.

The universal call to holiness is therefore no novelty of recent centuries. It is a divine imperative imprinted in human nature itself from creation, whose purpose is holiness, just as is that of redemption.

⟦p. 141⟧

All three divine persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, are engaged in both. To the Father is particularly attributed the notion of principle, the principle of every principle and of all reality, and therefore also of creation; to the Son, redemption; to the Holy Spirit, sanctification.

This distinction of functions is theologically logical. If holiness consists in the perfection of charity, as the Second Vatican Council puts it, the Holy Spirit is charity itself, the third Person of the Most Holy Trinity.

The Father created us; the Son redeemed us and made us children of God; the Holy Spirit sanctifies us by an ever-present action. His silent and discreet presence is recognised by the dynamism of love it arouses (cf. God's Gift…, pp. 101ff.).

Mother Rosa's experience testifies to the manifold workings of the Holy Spirit and urges us to cling lovingly to each divine person so as to become docile, as she was, to their initiative: “Those who let themselves be led by the Spirit of God are truly children of God” (cf. Rom 8:14); “Do you not know that you are God's temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (cf. 1 Cor 3:16).

Let us make our own, by contemplating them, all the attributes he made Mother Rosa experience: sanctifying grace, creative activity, fire of love, light that illumines minds and consciences, physician of souls, spiritual guide, tireless worker, voice that guides and directs in the work of the Father and of Jesus, inner strength, sweet consoler.

⟦p. 142⟧

Let us also often repeat the prayers to the Holy Spirit as the Church, teacher of prayer, invokes him in the Liturgy of the Holy Spirit: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love.”

And with his coming we shall experience that his action is the active and working presence of God's mercy in the soul, bound to the merits of Jesus the redeemer, in accordance with what the New Testament reveals to us.

1.4. The person docile to the action of grace attains the full maturity of Christ as a son in the Son

Docility to the action of the Spirit makes us new creatures, transformed into the image of Christ Jesus and ever more aware that we live in him, through him and with him the inheritance he won for us by offering himself as the victim of the new Covenant.

The Father himself illuminates this reality of ours through his Word: “The Holy Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if we truly share in his sufferings so as to share also in his glory. For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed in us” (Rom 8:16-18).

Since we must share in Christ's suffering, and since the Father knows our weakness, he does not leave us alone in our effort to identify with the Son, the firstborn of every human being.

⟦p. 143⟧

“The Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not even know what we ought to ask, but the Spirit himself intercedes insistently for us with groans too deep for words. He who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, for he intercedes for believers according to God's plan. We know, moreover, that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom he predestined he also glorified” (Rom 8:28-30).

Mother Rosa firmly believed in God's plan, and so she did not spare her life, always hoping, even against all hope, in him, her Good, her strength and her defender: “Who will accuse God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who will condemn? Jesus Christ, who died, or rather who was raised, is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us. Who then will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, distress, persecution, hunger, nakedness, danger or the sword?

As it is written: for your sake we are being killed all day long, we are treated as sheep for the slaughter.

But in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.”

⟦p. 145⟧

⟦p. 144⟧

This same certainty must grow in us, so that we may experience in our lives, in total surrender to the Father, how “neither death, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor anything else in all creation will ever be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom 8:38-39).

To be sons and daughters in the Son is our destiny, but it is still the object of our hope. “In hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he already sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Rom 8:24-25).

1.5. Holiness, the work of “divine Love”, which strengthens, sustains, frees, transforms and shapes

The Holy Spirit nourishes in us the hope of being freed from slavery to corruption and from the fear of sin, “to enter into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom 8:21).

Yes, the Holy Spirit guides us to freedom, to the whole truth, to holiness. The whole truth is Jesus: “I am the way, the truth and the life.” The Holy Spirit, who works ceaselessly, continues his descent into souls: on the day of Pentecost upon Mary Most Holy and the apostles, perceptibly and with a roar; ever since then gently and silently, to imprint on those who thirst for the love of God and for holiness the seal of the seven gifts: Wisdom, Understanding, Counsel, Fortitude, Knowledge, Piety and Fear of God, understood as fear of offending his love, fear of not responding generously to his desires.

The Holy Spirit continues always to descend and to work in people, producing his fruits in them:

“love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law” (Gal 5:22-23).

Pentecost, then, is not over; it continues in souls where it finds the assurance of hope, an insatiable thirst for perfection and a serious will to grow in the charity of which Saint Paul speaks (cf. 1 Cor 13:1ff.).

At this point one might say that everything on the way of holiness is the work of the Holy Spirit.

But everything is also the work of the Father: we have not received the spirit of a slave's servile fear but the spirit of adoption as children, in which we sigh: Abba, Father! The Holy Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (cf. Rom 8:15).

Everything, then, is also owed to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. From his divine fatherhood “every earthly human fatherhood and motherhood takes its origin and meaning” (Eph 3:15).

Not for nothing does Jesus speak continually of the Father, so much so that one day the Apostle Philip says to him: “Lord, show us the Father and we shall be satisfied.” And Jesus answers: “Have I been with you so long, and you do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (cf. John 14:8-10).

Everything, then, depends on the Father, everything depends on the Holy Spirit. It is no less true, however, that everything depends on the Son: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made of what exists” (John 1:3).

⟦p. 146⟧

In this connection let us also recall Saint Paul's prologue to the letters to the Ephesians, the Philippians and the Colossians.

Everything has been made and everything is worked by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Trinity of persons does not take away the unity of nature. The three divine persons are perfectly immanent in one another. The unity of nature does not take away the reality of the three Persons, their distinction and their distinct attributions. God thrice holy, thrice infinite love, thrice our creator and our redeemer.

This does not alter the fact that the supreme divine work is the Incarnation, through which the Son took human nature; the Word as man brought the divine nature close to us, so as to be called “God with us”. The most lovable face of the Redeemer and Saviour leads us into the great, ineffable mystery of the Most Holy Trinity.

Before this revealed truth, how can we fail to be deeply moved when we say the word Father! How can we fail to be moved before the Child born in Bethlehem of the Immaculate; how can we fail to be moved when we sing with the Church: “Come, O Creator Spirit, come, light of minds, come, Holy Spirit”, you who are the “Gift” par excellence, the Giver of all gifts.

“Come, we too implore,

Come, Holy Spirit,

make us your living temple!

Dwell

in us, pray in us, lead us to holiness,

⟦p. 147⟧

You are the infinite love of the Father and the Son, you, the infinite beatifying light.”

1.6. Mary, Daughter of Saint Anne, perfect model of docility to the action of the Holy Spirit

The supreme masterpiece of all masterpieces is the holiness of Mary Most Holy, so docile to the Holy Spirit, to his graces, gifts and inspirations, as to become his collaborator in the work of sanctifying souls.

Mary Most Holy is not only a masterpiece to admire and contemplate, but a presence to prolong and a model to embody. She is the active collaborator of the Holy Spirit, the living and eloquent example and unsurpassable teacher of docility to his action, the most perfect imitator of the Son, most obedient to the Father's will.

After Jesus, the way, the truth and the life, in the work of our sanctification we look to Mary Most Holy, our Mother in the order of grace.

Mother Rosa's experience:

“O Mary, through you I am saved, through you I am a religious. The fire of love of your Son, Mary, you kindled many times with your own hands in this heart of your Son” (Memoirs 4.4, p. 56)

⟦p. 148⟧

reveals how much she trusted in Mary's motherly intercession and how she contemplated her as daughter of Saint Anne, the perfect model of docility to the Spirit, who made her the perfect image of Jesus her Son, the Poor One, in whom “the Father was well pleased”.

2.1. The Church, sacrament, sign,

instrument of intimate union with God

and of the unity of the whole human race (LG 1)

The outpouring of the Holy Spirit gives rise to the new and renewing reality of the Church, trustee of the work of redemption, guardian of the merits of Jesus, an inexhaustible source of the descent of the Holy Spirit with all the richness of his gifts.

The outpouring of the Spirit unifies the Church, making the “people of God” one body, the “mystical body of Jesus”, the whole Christ.

Baptism makes all the baptised members of a single body.

⟦p. 149⟧

In all the Sacraments the Holy Spirit works for the unity of the Church, especially in the Eucharist, which is at once the consecration and the surpassing of the world. Consecration, because it is an earthly gesture performed on humble earthly things woven into our daily existence. Surpassing, because the Eucharist places within our earthly condition a foretaste of the heavenly condition and transforms the community of believers gathered with Christ at the altar into a community above time, immersed in mystery, set on the plane of the Parousia, that is, of the coming of Jesus in glory.

We cannot, therefore, grow in love for the Son of God except through knowledge and love of the Church. The Church and Christ are not adequately distinct. The Church is identified with the “mystery hidden for ages in God”. Her reality, like that of the glorious Jesus, is therefore in harmony with the divine wisdom that conceived her, and so it exceeds our capacity to understand. That is why we should not be surprised if we have to use a multiplicity of concepts, all merely approximate, which at times almost seem to contradict one another. In fact we are dealing with the mysterious richness of her reality, which we are invited to meditate upon.

The Church, according to the Second Vatican Council, is “the image of the invisible God”.

Wonderfully prepared in the history of the people of Israel and in the old Covenant and established in the last times, she was made manifest by the outpouring of the Spirit and will reach her glorious completion at the end of the ages. Then, as we read in the holy Fathers, all the just from Adam onwards, “from Abel the just to the last of the elect”, will be gathered with the Father in the universal Church (cf. LG 2).

The earthly, visible Church and the invisible heavenly Church are distinct but inseparable. It is one and the same Church.

“To carry out the Father's will, Christ inaugurated the kingdom of heaven on earth, revealed to us his mystery and by his obedience brought about re-

⟦p. 150⟧

demption. The Church, that is, the kingdom of Christ already present in mystery by the power of God, grows visibly in the world. This beginning and this growth are signified by the blood and water that flowed from the opened side of the crucified Christ, and are foretold by the Lord's words about his death on the cross: ‘And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all to myself’ (John 12:32). Each time the sacrifice of the cross, ‘by which Christ our Passover Lamb has been sacrificed’ (1 Cor 5:7), is celebrated on the altar, the work of our redemption is renewed. And at the same time, in the sacrament of the Eucharistic bread, the unity of the faithful, who form one body in Christ, is represented and brought about; he is the light of the world, from him we come, through him we live, towards him we are directed” (LG 3).

In this truly wonderful sense Jesus is our hope, and the Church is truly the Ark of the Covenant, prefigured in the old Covenant and divinely realised in the new and eternal Covenant.

The Church is therefore the beginning on earth of the kingdom of Christ and of God.

⟦p. 151⟧

In the light of this splendid theology of the Church the various images of the Church outlined by the Council become luminously clear: “the Church is the sheepfold whose one gate is Christ; she is the flock of which Christ himself is the Good Shepherd and the prince of shepherds; she is God's field, in which grows the ancient olive tree whose holy root was the patriarchs…; the Church is God's building, of which the Lord is the cornerstone, the foundation on which the Church herself is built and from which she will receive stability and cohesion. The Church is the house where his family dwells, God's dwelling among men; she is the new Jerusalem, the Holy City. In her we, as living stones, form a spiritual temple. Saint John in the Apocalypse contemplates this holy city in its final stage, coming down from God like a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev 21:1ff.).

The Church is the heavenly Jerusalem, “our mother”, the immaculate bride of the immaculate Lamb.

And while the Church makes her pilgrimage on this earth far from the Lord (cf. 2 Cor 5:6), she is like an exile who seeks and longs for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, until she appears clothed in glory with her Bridegroom (cf. Col 3:1-4)” (cf. LG 6, 7). The image par excellence, however, is the Church as the mystical body formed by Christ and believers (cf. LG 7). After this whole series of attributes, the Council also devotes a chapter to “the Church as the people of God”. And this is most true, provided we do not forget what it has already said about the “mystical body”.

In the heavenly Church the unity of the Church with Christ, in Christ and through Christ will appear more clearly, that is, the unity of the Church in the Most Holy Trinity through the work of the Holy Spirit. According to the best theologians, then, the Church is above all the body of the Lord, the bride of Christ, the sacrament of intimate union with God, the “Icon” of the Most Holy Trinity in the image of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, a holy and immaculate bride (cf. Eph 5:27).

⟦p. 152⟧

2.2. In the Church,

the one vocation of all the baptised

The Church is holy because her members are baptised, and Saint Paul calls the baptised “saints” (cf. Titus 3:5; Eph 5:26; 1 Cor 6:11).

Thanks to baptism, the Spirit of the Father and the Son is reflected upon them.

The Council devotes Chapter II of Lumen Gentium to the Church as the “people of God”.

“Christ the Lord, high priest taken from among men (cf. Heb 5:1-5), made the new people ‘a kingdom of priests to God his Father’ (Rev 1:6; cf. 5:9-10). Through regeneration and the anointing of the Holy Spirit the baptised are consecrated to form a spiritual temple and a holy priesthood, so that through all the works of a Christian they may offer spiritual sacrifices and proclaim the wonders of him who called them out of darkness into his marvellous light (cf. 1 Pet 2:4-10). Therefore all the disciples of Christ, persevering in prayer and praising God together (cf. Acts 2:42-47), should offer themselves as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God (cf. Rom 12:1), bear witness to Christ everywhere and give to anyone who asks a reason for the hope of eternal life that is in them (cf. 1 Pet 3:15)” (LG 10). Just as all people are called to Christianity, so they are actually and virtually called to the Catholic Church.

⟦p. 153⟧

“The people of God also share in Christ's prophetic office by spreading everywhere a living witness to him, above all through a life of faith and charity, and when it offers a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that acclaim his name (Heb 13:15)” (LG 12). The Church, made up of the baptised and of believers, is on her part always holy (as we profess in the Creed) and sanctifying. Indeed, not even sin destroys in the sinner the sanctifying effect of baptism: the seed and root of a possible return to God and of consequent sanctification.

The holiness of the Church has its icon in Mary Most Holy, the Immaculate. And just as the Immaculate is the Mother of the Word made man, so the Church continually, through the sacraments, begets and regenerates holiness, thanks to her indissoluble union with Christ, her most holy bridegroom, the Holy One by essence, the first principle of all holiness: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

The Most Holy Trinity, in Christ and through Christ the redeemer, is the first source of all holiness, which is “the work of Divine love” that strengthens, sustains, frees, transforms and shapes those who share in it with faith through the sacraments, above all penance and the Eucharist.

The sacrament of penance is a powerful means of sanctification, renewal and new beginning, in which Jesus purifies souls in his Blood of infinite value.

⟦p. 154⟧

⟦p. 155⟧

Each time a soul approaches this sacrament with repentance and humbly confesses its sin, Jesus purifies it, gives it peace with itself, renews it inwardly, sets it back on the way of holiness, fills it ever anew with fresh graces and spiritual energies, and pours into it peace, serenity, spiritual joy and renewed ardour for perfection.

The person docile to the action of grace, of which the sacraments are an inexhaustible source, attains the full maturity of Christ, as a son in the Son (cf. Eph 4:13). This happens in a wonderful and most effective way in the Eucharist, especially in the encounter in which Jesus transforms souls in the measure of their openness, makes them one with himself and renders them strong and invincible.

The Eucharistic bread is the “living” and life-giving “bread” because it is the flesh and blood not of a mere man but of the incarnate Word: a bread that brings into the soul all the fullness and infinite sanctifying richness of his divinity.

In the Eucharist the sacraments find their completion through the living presence of Jesus Christ himself, the author, cause and end of all the sacraments.

The Eucharist is the new Covenant, no longer merely a pact but Jesus Christ himself, who renews his Covenant not only with us but within us, until he transfigures us into himself.

The Eucharist expresses the fullness of God's goodness, wisdom and power, and is the sign of Jesus' ultimate self-giving, which seals the new and eternal Covenant for time and for eternity.

3.1. Called to holiness

in identification with the poor Christ, contemplated in Mary

After the long waiting for the promise, we see the Covenant concentrated in the family of Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate, and in a special way in the person of Mary, who marks the dawn of the Redemption.

The personalisation of the Covenant therefore reaches its furthest creaturely limit in Mary Most Holy, whose birth is a proclamation of joy for the whole universe.

Mary Most Holy is the mother of the new Covenant by the very fact that she is Mother of the eternal Word, of God-with-us. Thus is fulfilled the indissoluble Covenant of the divine nature with human nature in Jesus Christ, a divine person, in whom the Covenant coincides with the mystery of the incarnation. Two natures, the divine and the human, become one person: the divine person of the Word.

God sealed the Covenant in a truly divine way: a God who becomes Man; a man who is God!

Jesus Christ prolongs this personal unity in the mystery of the Eucharist, as if to unite to himself each person in the Church, the new people of God, so intimately united to him, its divine head, as members of the one body, the mystical body.

⟦p. 156⟧

Personal or community participation in the Eucharistic Sacrifice, which is the Mass, is a celebration of the new Covenant.

In this loving plan of the faithful and merciful God, Jesus Christ becomes not only Teacher but divine builder of holiness for all the members of his mystical body, the people of God.

And Mother Rosa, living the Eucharist intensely, could exclaim with her life: “It is no longer I who live. It is Jesus Christ who lives in me.” In this sense the Covenant reaches its fullness in the individual as a member of the mystical body of Jesus.

But besides the Eucharist, Jesus Christ willed to give his followers and friends a model of docility to grace in Mary Most Holy, Daughter of Saint Anne, as our Mother, a masterpiece of docility and readiness to the action of the Holy Spirit.

The whole Church is called to holiness on the model of Mary Most Holy, the figure of the Church herself, to such a degree that the attributes of Mary's supreme holiness are given to the Church.

She is the new Eve. But with what a difference! Her fullness of grace incomparably transcends the holiness of the angels and saints because of her unique relationship of intimacy with God.

⟦p. 157⟧

It is the divine motherhood: “Even before her birth God flooded her with grace, immersing her in the possession of all original justice, placing her far above the grace of our first parents while still innocent, above the just Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. None of these was favoured by God with a relationship even remotely like that with which he favoured Mary” (Gherardini B., La Madre, Frigento 1990, p. 342).

Under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, Pope Paul VI declared Mary Most Holy “Mother of the Church”.

Mary Most Holy is not only a member of the Church: she is her Mother. If the Church, as mystical body, is the “whole Christ”, Mary Most Holy is undoubtedly Mother of the Church, also called by theologians the “Ark of the new Covenant”.

Mary, then, is the mother of the new Covenant, the one who lives and brings to fulfilment the spirituality of the Covenant and of hope that is characteristic of Mother Rosa's great Family.

The Covenant by its nature invites and leads to hope in all its fullness: not only hope in the return of Jesus Christ at the moment of our death, and not only in his glorious return at the end of time, but also in his progressive return, which becomes an ever more living, felt and visible presence in a faith that grows day by day in souls reaching out towards holiness and the perfection of charity.

⟦p. 158⟧

⟦p. 159⟧

Here, then, the title of this chapter takes on its full meaning. It is a matter of the charism of the foundress Mother Rosa Gattorno, a true spiritual doctrine distinct and proper to a religious Family that expresses in the life of the Church a very precise particular dimension, magnificently contained in the very name of the Institute, “Daughters [and Sons] of Saint Anne”, mother of the Immaculate, mother of the Ark of the Covenant, of her who perfectly unites and unfolds the old and the new Covenant.

3.2. In the wake of Mother Rosa

in consecrated and lay life

In the light of what has been said, the call to holiness in identification with the humble and poor Christ, from Bethlehem to Calvary and to the Eucharist, becomes clear, along the path traced and lived by Mother Rosa, both in consecrated life, as a sign of future goods in the Church and in the world, and in lay life, as a leaven of life and a witness of charity. Yes! The universal vocation to holiness is the same for all, but the style and programme to be carried out differ in the various religious families, and distinct is the Spirit who guides both the consecrated souls and the lay people who follow the unrepeatable charism proper to the foundress, within the identity of the one paradigm.

Ultimately it is always the same Jesus Christ who is to be imitated. But the infinite riches of the Redeemer's holiness, wisdom and virtues allow a variety of charisms that are never mere conformity. All charisms are “imitation” of and “identification” with Christ, yet all are authentically original and unrepeatable, both in the community and in the personal sense. Every charism is a generous outpouring, ever new and distinct, of the “unsearchable riches of Christ”; every charism is a new and original proclamation of Christ which all his followers are called to make shine “before the eyes of all, in fulfilment of the mystery hidden for ages in the mind of God, creator of the universe, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known in heaven to the principalities and powers, according to the eternal purpose he has realised in Christ Jesus our Lord, who gives us the courage to approach God with full confidence through faith in him” (Eph 3:8-12).

Here we enter the depths of Christ's charity. “For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be mightily strengthened by his Spirit in the inner man. May Christ dwell in your hearts through faith, so that, rooted and grounded in charity, you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses all knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. To him who is able to do far more than we can ask or think, according to the power at work within us, to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, for ever and ever” (Eph 3:14-21).

Mother Rosa Gattorno entered these depths of the love of God with firm will and enlightened generosity. In her footsteps the way to holiness lies smooth, both for all the members of her spiritual Family and for those who follow her teaching and example.

⟦p. 160⟧

Mother Rosa's own charism splendidly eases the way towards holiness, the goal of human, Christian and religious life.

Mother Rosa entered the mystery of Christ's charity and advanced wonderfully to the highest degrees of the spiritual life, penetrating the wisdom of the cross in a way not unlike Paul's experience:

“When I came to you, brothers, I did not come proclaiming the testimony of God with lofty words or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.

I came among you in weakness and in much fear and trembling; and my speech and my message did not rest on persuasive words of wisdom, but on the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (cf. 1 Cor 2:1-5.10).

Mother Rosa reached the highest degrees of mystical life by walking again the way of Calvary: “the Crucified” Jesus, in the mystery of his poverty, was her “Good”.

This is the surest way of spiritual progress and holiness.

⟦p. 161⟧

Her apostolic zeal for the good and salvation of souls – “I would like to run everywhere and cry out aloud so that everyone may come to love you, and I would like to have a thousand lives to spend them all…” – rested on these most solid foundations. Suffering and the cross, accepted and lived with love and out of love, lay at the origin of that joyful serenity of spirit she left as an inheritance to her spiritual daughters and sons.

The labours of the apostolate and sufferings of every kind did not extinguish but kept alive the joyful inner and outer serenity proper to the saints. “I am filled with comfort and joy in all our affliction” (2 Cor 7:4).

This is one of Mother Rosa's most distinctive characteristics, left as an inheritance to all the members of the Family of the holy mother of the Immaculate.

These are unmistakable characteristics that mark the holiness and apostolate of Mother Rosa and of all who follow her spirit.

Mother Rosa's charism, left as an inheritance to her spiritual Family, has the great advantage of unifying the Christian spiritual life in a truly admirable way. The unifying principle is Jesus the redeemer, object and goal of the Covenant and of hope: Jesus Christ, the One who was to come in the hope of the old Covenant; Jesus Christ who has come, who is the Covenant and hope made a divine-human person, the supreme manifestation of the mercy of God the Father who sends the Son, teacher and model of all holiness, through the active presence of the Holy Spirit.

⟦p. 162⟧

Life within the most blessed Trinity, increased day after day, knows no limits. Holiness, in the soul that takes seriously the great treasure of the life of grace, knows no other conclusion than progress, an ever deeper entering into the fullness of God's own life, which every day and every hour transfigures the soul, intoxicating it with divinity.

This is the God of the new Covenant, ever more ardently loved and hoped for until the beatifying unveiling of eternal life.

Mother Rosa, having advanced with great strides in the love of God and neighbour, was enriched with much wisdom, which, according to Saint Thomas, is the very love of God (Saint Thomas, Commentary on the Gospel of Saint John, ch. XV, v. 8).

“With the ardour of charity the knowledge of truth is communicated” (Ibid., ch. V, v. 6, III).

The love of God, experienced in uncommon measure by Mother Rosa, was the space in which she moved, letting the Most Holy Trinity – breaking in upon her – fill and transform her life:

“Great mystery! Oh, if only I could make you known to the whole world! You, if one may say so, are mad for man; and he, alas!… A voice that says to me:

  • Yes, I love him, but my love is not returned!

⟦p. 163⟧

As he said this, he came so close that I felt myself enraptured. O sanctifying Spirit, divine Essence, ever ready to pour yourself into the ungrateful hearts of men! What precious nectar breathes from a single drop that man might come to taste! O sweetness beyond compare! Oh, whoever comes to taste and possess that divine Essence, surely all that is earthly serves him only as nausea.

The intellect, opened by divine power, communes with his immortal Being and, in that infinite ocean of infinite greatness, understands all things, is blessed and delights in Love. Oh, how infinite you are in your despotic, absolute power! and then, beloved Father and Spouse of hearts. O strength of loving souls and of all who live in you and for you!” (M 1.2, p. 1f.).

And since no creature has ever loved God as much as Mary Most Holy, also because of the absolutely unique mission God gave her in the plan of Redemption, the Church invokes her as seat of wisdom, not only because she is the mother of God, but because she loved God as no one has ever loved him or ever will.

The virtue of love of God and neighbour therefore unites heaven and earth, time and eternity, and so it will never pass away. It can grow indefinitely during our mortal life, but it will find its fullness in heaven, when we see God as he is.
